blocks.text: Abstract

This study evaluates the effectiveness of an innovative tertiary stress management intervention for workplace application, combining 0. 1 Hz coherent breathing with blue light exposure via the ÉOS device.  We hypothesize that the intervention can mitigate acute stress reactions and sleepiness more effectively than passive rest without external stimulation.  Using a randomized-controlled crossover double-blind design in a workplace-based laboratory setting, we assessed the effect of an intervention following exposition to Maastricht Acute Stress Test in 29 individuals.  Subjective stress (single item scale), sleepiness (Karolinska Sleepiness Scale), positive and negative affect (Positive and Negative Affect Schedule), along with heart rate variability (HRV) and electroencephalography metrics were evaluated using linear mixed-effect models.  The intervention significantly reduced subjective stress by 31. 23% (CI 21. 41% and 41. 83%), decreased sleepiness by 0. 84 points (SE 0. 17), and increased positive affect by 1. 85 points (SE 0. 54).  No significant effect was found on negative affect, HRV, frontal alpha asymmetry or theta/beta ratio.

The findings suggest that combining coherent breathing with blue light exposure effectively reduces acute stress and enhances mood without causing sleepiness, making it a promising workplace stress intervention.  This study contributes to stress management research by demonstrating the potential of these tertiary stress management interventions to improve well-being and performance in occupational settings.  Future research should evaluate the individual effects of each component, examine long-term outcomes, and include diverse populations to strengthen these findings.
Introduction

The dynamics of stress and work significantly influence individuals’ lives. Work, either in a standard 9-to-5 job, self-employment, or shift work, is a major stress source. Chronic stress with longer-term impact [1] is well known for being related to health issues, productivity losses, absences, early retirement, and substantial economic costs ranging from millions to billions of dollars [2–7]. Acute stress, lasting minutes or hours, increases arousal and influences cognitive functions [8] which is critical for optimal performance. However, inadequate coping and overload can compromise employees’ well-being, performance, and safety [9,10]. This relationship gains added significance when considering high-risk occupations such as first responders, military, firefighters, police, and astronauts [11–14]. Given these considerations, exploring effective stress management solutions applicable at workplace becomes imperative for employers who want to provide resources for active stress management, optimize workers’ performance, achieve a competitive advantage [5] and for those who care about imposing a positive impact on health and society.

According to Lamontagne et al. [15], stress interventions are categorized as primary (preventive, targeting the work environment and worker behaviors), secondary (enhancing self-efficacy through skills training, education, and coaching), or tertiary (reactive, mitigating stress impacts). Most individual interventions fall into the primary or secondary categories, with a gap in tertiary group interventions [5,15–18]. These interventions typically address chronic rather than acute stress [9] and often involve relaxation, mindfulness, or cognitive-behavioral approaches. Cognitive-behavioral interventions are generally more effective than relaxation or mindfulness, both often part of preventive programs [2,6,17,19]. However, there is limited information on the use of relaxation techniques as a tertiary strategy, their impact on the stress response or outcomes relevant for workplace performance, as interventions may inadvertently increase sleepiness or reduce post-relaxation performance readiness.

Interventions using external stimuli, such as blue light, show promise in balancing stress responses and sleepiness [20]. Blue light’s influence on mood and cognitive functions is well-documented, primarily through its modulation of intrinsically photosensitive retinal ganglion cells (ipRGCs), which connect to brain regions regulating circadian rhythms and sleep [21–24]. Although blue light has been shown to increase alertness, its acute effects on post-exposure arousal and behavioral alertness are mixed [23,25,26]. The ipRGCs also influence mood and cognitive functions by connecting to brain areas involved in emotion processing [24,27–30]. Blue light’s effect on mood may involve physiological reactions affecting neurotransmitter and hormone production [31]. Studies have observed accelerated relaxation and decreased heart rate variability ratios with blue light exposure, suggesting its potential for stress management across diverse populations. Minguillon et al. [20] observed accelerated relaxation using blue light in a chromotherapy room, impacting subjective stress and gamma brainwaves. Similarly, Yuda et al. [26,32] found a reduction in the high frequency (HF) HRV band and the low to high frequency (LF/HF) HRV ratio in response to blue light. However, Choi et al. [33] did not find significant effects on most HRV variables in their study. Taken together, it could be assumed that blue light activates brain areas involved in emotion processing and, when combined with relaxation techniques, may expedite acute stress recovery.

A candidate technique that can be combined with blue light is coherent breathing, achieved through slow and controlled breathing at a 0.1 Hz frequency (six respiration cycles a minute with a one-to-one ratio). A review by Sevoz-Couche & Laborde [34] describes that coherent breathing results in in-phase cardiac oscillations and out-of-phase blood pressure oscillations. These physiological modifications lead to an increase in HRV through vagal efferent enhancement with various positive effects on cognition and stress (Sevoz-Couche & Laborde, 2022). A study on air traffic controllers suggests that biofeedback coherent breathing may be effective in preventing fatigue and the related decrease in cognitive function [35]. Furthermore, some evidence suggests that an environmental light has significant impact on the regulation of breathing through direct signalling in the intrinsically photosensitive retinal circuitry to the suprachiasmatic nucleus pathway [36], possibly further aiding with the ease of physiology modulation.

These studies expose several research gaps and limitations in current literature, including a lack of theoretical basis, neutral control groups, and small sample sizes with fewer than 20 participants, which undermine internal validity and robustness [17,23,25,26,34,37,38]. There is also a scarcity of studies on tertiary intervention strategies for mitigating already-occurred stress [9,17]. Furthermore, the research lacks investigations into using external stimuli to enhance relaxation and assessments of both subjective and objective markers of sleepiness and stress [1,39,40]. Addressing these gaps is crucial for enhancing stress management and developing effective workplace interventions to support employee well-being.

The primary objective of this study is to evaluate the effectiveness of an innovative tertiary (reactive) stress management intervention that addresses the identified gaps in the existing literature. The intervention integrates coherent breathing guided by an external blue light stimulus, delivered by the ÉOS device — a multisensory recovery system developed by Human design Group designed for fatigue and stress management in occupational settings, offering calibrated sessions adaptable to the user’s state and recovery goals — in a Research & Development (R&D) laboratory within Human design Group’s office. The study hypothesizes that the applied reactive stress countermeasure will more effectively mitigate acute stress reactions and sleepiness, compared to passive rest without external stimulation. In this randomized-controlled cross-over double blinded design, parameters are measured through both subjective and objective markers. These markers include questionnaires and measurements of heart rate variability using root mean square successive difference (rMSSD), low-frequency band (LF), and electroencephalography (EEG) of frontal alpha asymmetry (FAA) and theta/beta ratio (S1.4) [41].
Materials and methods
Participants

The analysed sample consisted of 58 observations from 29 individuals (32 from 16 women, and 26 from 13 men) who underwent both control and experimental conditions. The mean age was 28.72 (SD = 8.56) years with a positive skew towards younger people under 34 years. All participants were based in France, majority of them were of French nationality and all had completed at least high-school education. During the first session, men’s average body mass index (BMI) was 23.32 (SD = 3.46), and woman’s 22.88 (SD = 3.63). Of all participants, 82.76% reported being non-smokers. The data on anthropometrics and potential confounders are available in the supplementary materials (S3.1. Questionnaires).
Sampling procedure and exclusion criteria

The study was approved by the CER (Research Ethics Committee) at the Université Fédérale, Toulouse Midi-Pyrénées N° 00011835-2023-0328-648- Université Fédérale de Toulouse IRB # 1. We recruited 30 participants, based on an a priori power analysis (see the Sample size and power calculation section below). Invitations for self-selection to participate as a volunteer were sent by e-mail to employees and interns of Human design Group, SpaceshipFR based at the Centre national d’études spatiales (CNES), and ISAE-SUPAERO. The measurement phase was executed at Human design Group’s R&D laboratory. Participants signed the informed consent document at the beginning of the study, before the first measurement.

Exclusion criteria were cardiovascular anomalies detectable by electrocardiography (ECG), cardiovascular diseases, severe physical illnesses (e.g., fibromyalgia), hypertension, endocrine disorders, current or previous psychopathology, substance abuse, heavy smoking (>10 cigarettes/day) or being on any kind of medication known to affect the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis (more details in Ráčková et al. [41]; based on Smeets et al. [42]).
Sample size and power calculation

The minimum required number of individuals was 26, given the power = 0.80, alpha = 0.05, effect size = 0.59, and correlation between measures = 0.85 (calculated for repeated measures ANOVA, between factors using G*Power, see S 1.1. Sample size for further details). We aimed to recruit 30 individuals (15 in each group) to account for potential dropouts. The analysed sample consisted of 58 observations from 29 individuals (15 in intervention first – control second, and 14 in control first – intervention second groups).
Study design

This study was a two-arm, randomized, controlled, crossover design, developed using the Experimental Design Assistant [43]. An AB/BA design with computer-generated 1:1 block randomization was used [44,45], with the algorithm assigning participants to the ÉOS or control intervention. The researcher could not predict group allocations, as they were unaware of the intervention assigned to each participant’s ID. The treatment periods were separated by 3 weeks to prevent carry-over effects [46]. Data analysts were blinded to the order of interventions to minimize bias [47]. The assessment followed several experimental stages, consistent with previous recommendations [39], and the study reporting adhered to the Consolidated Standards of Reporting Trials (CONSORT) statement [48].
Interventions

Participants were reminded of a scheduled appointment via email one week prior to the experiment and were provided with the following instructions: maintain a regular sleep routine, abstain from alcohol and vigorous physical activity for the 24 hours prior to the test, refrain from consuming food, coffee, or smoking for the 2 hours prior to the test, and bring appropriate clothing and personal hygiene items.

Upon arrival, participants underwent anthropometric measurements and completed demographic questionnaires (only in the first session). Physiological measurement hardware (EEG and ECG) was then mounted. Baseline questionnaires on confounders, Subjective stress, Karolinska Sleepiness Scale (KSS), and Positive and Negative Affect Schedule (PANAS) were administered in both sessions. A 5-minute baseline physiological data collection followed, with participants sitting calmly, knees at a 90° angle, feet flat on the floor, hands on thighs, and eyes closed.

Participants then underwent the Maastricht Acute Stress Task (MAST), involving an anticipation phase and a stress task with cold water immersion, mental arithmetic, and social evaluation [42]. After the MAST, participants completed questionnaires on subjective stress, KSS, and PANAS. They were then transferred to the ÉOS room to recline on a bed with an elevated back and engage in a relaxation intervention. This involved either exposure to the ÉOS program with blue light and sound cues for coherent breathing, or, for the control group, lying on a bed in complete darkness without any additional stimuli. The final round of questionnaires on Subjective stress, KSS, and PANAS was then administered. The experiment concluded with the removal of physiological devices, and participants were allowed to leave.

All experimental manipulations and measurement were conducted by 2 deliverers (Lucie Ráčková and Inès Butin) with proper training. Training on EEG was delivered by Emma Chabani with Ph.D. in neuroscience and prior experience in EEG measurement. Training on HRV, anthropometry and questionnaires was delivered by Lucie Ráčková, Ph.D. candidate in environmental physiology and MSc. in Anthropology with previous experience in these methods. Training on the MAST was delivered by the authors of the method [42]. More details on the experimental manipulation, including time taken, are detailed in previously published research protocol [49].
Methods
ÉOS system

The ÉOS device delivers multisensory recovery sessions through two main components: a LED lighting system emitting calibrated wavelengths of light according to the session scenario and recovery goal, and a spatialized sound environment providing auditory guidance for coherent breathing, meditation, or relaxation. Sessions are calibrated based on the user’s state (fatigue or stress), the selected duration, and relaxation preferences, with or without sleep. In the present study, all participants underwent both the experimental and control conditions as part of the crossover design. In the experimental condition, a single standardized 15-minute relaxation scenario without sleep was assigned by the researchers, during which coherent breathing was guided at 5.5 cycles per minute (0.1 Hz) through synchronized light pulses and auditory cues. Participants did not select or modify any session parameters. The specific parameters of the light and sound stimuli are proprietary.
Anthropometry

Upon arrival to their first trial, participants’ weight was measured using the Mi Body Composition Scale 2 (Xiaomi Communications Co., Ltd.), and their height was measured using a wall-mounted retractable measuring tape (Yuecoom) with precision to 0.1 cm. The measurement followed the definition from Anthropometry Procedures Manual of National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey [50]. Circumferences were measured using the measuring tape included in the Nox A1s Polysomnograph (Nox Medial USA, Alpharetta, United States) with precision to 0.1 cm. Definitions of measurements followed the WHO STEPwise Approach to Surveillance (STEPS) and can be found in the Waist Circumference and Waist-Hip Ratio report of the WHO Expert Consultation [51].
Questionnaires
Over the course of the study, participants were administered several questionnaires:

Demographic and confounders were assessed using a form from Laborde et al. [52], modified by requirements from the ethics committee. We asked specifically about: age, gender, smoking, habitual alcohol intake, weight, height, waist-hip ratio, use of cardioactive medication and contraceptives, the prior night’s sleep routine, any intensive physical training 24h prior to the experiment, intake of food or caffeinated drinks 2h before the experiment, alcohol intake 24h prior to the experiment, and the necessity to go to the bathroom.
Subjective stress is a simple scale ranging from 1 to 10 where participants rated how stressed they felt at that moment. This approach has been used in several studies with good sensitivity [53].

Positive and Negative Affect Schedule (PANAS) is a scale evaluating a person’s affect using a 20-item 5-point Likert scale, providing overall scoring for both Positive (PA) and Negative Affect (NA) [54]. We used the French version; the psychometric properties are tested elsewhere [55].

Karolinska Sleepiness Scale (KSS) is a single question 9-point Likert scale measuring current sleepiness level, previously used in studies of shift work, attention, and performance [56], validated in a study using EEG data [57]. We used a French translation of this item.
Physiological measurements
Participants’ physiological signals were measured using the following devices:

Electrocardiography (ECG) – our study used bipolar ECG electrodes from the Nox A1s Polysomnograph (Nox Medial USA, Alpharetta, United States) with ±1024mV input range, < 3 µVrms noise, 512 kHz sampling rate, 24-bit AD.

Electroencephalography (EEG) – our study used 8 unipolar EEG electrodes from the Nox A1s Polysomnograph (Nox Medial USA, Alpharetta, United States) with ±3.2mV input range < 1 µVrms noise, 512 kHz sampling rate. Electrodes were placed in the areas close to Fp1, Fp2, F3, F4, CZ, and PZ on the scalp and, according to the 10–20 international system, at E1 and E2 around the eyes as a polysomnographic montage. The left/right mastoid (M1 and M2) electrodes were used as lateral reference for the right/left electrodes respectively, while an electrode placed on Fpz was used as a ground.
Data preprocessing
ECG.

As a first step, R-peaks were identified and manually corrected in the ECG time-series using R-DECO [58,59]. R-DECO is an open-source project developed in Matlab specifically for semi-automatic detection of R-peaks and hence, the calculation of R-R intervals. First, an enveloping procedure is used to flatten the ECG signal while enhancing the QRS complexes [60].

Then, a rule-based algorithm along with the Pan-Tompkins algorithm is used to detect the R-peaks in the flattened time-series [58,61]. A first automatic correction of the peaks is performed using a search-back procedure [62]. Using this processing method, the author reported about 99% of correctly detected peaks [58]. However, erroneous or mis-positioned peaks can be present after processing, especially for recording with a high level of noise. For this reason, R-DECO includes a graphical user interface that can be used to correct for algorithm errors by manually adding, removing or adjusting the R-peaks. Quality control of R-peak detection was ensured through systematic visual inspection of the entire ECG time series for each participant by a trained operator, who manually corrected any flagged or visually identified anomalies. A final review of the corrected series was performed to confirm the absence of residual errors prior to HRV feature extraction. This procedure was applied uniformly across all participants and sessions.

The corrected R-R intervals series was then used to calculate HRV features using an in-house script and dedicated python libraries. The root means squared of successive differences (RMSSD) was calculated using the hrv_time function of the neurokit2 library [63]. The power densities of low frequencies, high frequencies, and their ratio were calculated using the hrvanalysis library [64,65]. The features of interest were calculated for each period of interest by segmenting the time R-R intervals time series based on the timestamp at the beginning and end of each period (e.g., baseline, MAST instructions, MAST task, first half of ÉOS, second half of ÉOS, post ÉOS).
EEG.

EEG data were processed in Python using the mne library [66,67]. First, raw data were filtered using a digital band-pass filter (0.1–70 Hz) to remove physiologically implausible frequencies, combined with a notch filter at 50 Hz and 100 Hz to remove noise related to alternating current. Then, power spectral density was calculated using the multitaper method [68] over the entire signal length using 2-second windows with an overlap of one second. The integral over the different EEG rhythms was used to calculate the relative power spectral density (PSD) of each rhythm (alpha: 8–13 Hz, beta: 13–30 Hz, delta: 1–4 Hz, gamma: 30–70 Hz, theta: 4–8 Hz). Then, the values from the 2-second windows were averaged over the period of interest in order to have one value for each rhythm for each period of interest.

Pre-processed data served as a base for calculation of the metrics of interest. First, FAA was calculated by subtracting the natural log of left hemisphere alpha power (F3_M2) from the natural log of right hemisphere alpha power (F4_M1) [69] for each experiment phase and used as a predictor value, in line with recommendations of [70]. Second, the theta/beta ratio was calculated for each period by dividing PSD of the theta power calculated under FP1 by PSD of the beta power calculated under FP1 (resulting in Theta/Beta FP1 variable) and PSD of the theta power calculated under FP2 by PSD of the beta power calculated under FP2 (resulting in Theta/Beta FP2 variable).
Data analysis

Anonymized data used as input for the analysis script, which allowed us to generate the supplementary material file with RMarkdown is available on Zenodo (https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.20596627 or https://zenodo.org/records/20596627). Code for analysis is in the Supplementary Materials.
Software

An a priori power analysis was performed using G*Power 3.1.9.7 [71]. All other analyses were conducted using RStudio version 2023.12.1.402 [72]. Used packages including citations are in S 8. Package information.
Repeated measures ANOVA

Repeated measures ANOVA (rmANOVA) was used to examine the assumptions of the study, e.g., correct randomization and absence of carry-over effects. We checked the assumptions of the rmANOVA by investigating for sphericity using Mauchly’s test implemented in the anova_test function from the rstatix library in R [73] and for normality using the Shapiro-Wilk test using the shapiro_test function from the rstatix library [73] and Q-Q plots using the ggqqplot function within the ggpubr library in R [74]. Significant outliers were identified using the identify_outliers function from the rstatix library in R [73] and were removed from analysis. However, remaining violations of normality were described in the supplementary material and not further addressed here as recent studies showed that rmANOVA is generally robust to them [75].
Linear mixed-effect models

Linear Mixed-Effect Models (LMEM) were checked for normal distribution of residuals and random effects deviation by plotting residuals and random effects along with the models. Some dependent variables were log-transformed to improve homoskedasticity. Since log-transformation changes the scale of the data, we report confidence intervals (CI) instead of standard errors (SE) for the transformed variables. Some of the models were also improved by identifying outliers using the identify_outliers function from the rstatix library in R [73] and retaining only those within the range defined by 1.5 times the interquartile range above the third quartile and below the first quartile. Due to the repeated measures design, participant ID was selected as a random effect in all models. Model comparison was conducted by first modelling full models with all of the predictors which we defined as critical during the literature review for this study. We also checked for multicollinearity by examining strong correlations within predictors. Given the limited sample size and Occam’s razor principle, we removed non-significant predictors which did not influence model fit. Successive models differ only in fixed effects. Model comparison was guided by Bayesian Information Criterion (BIC), also considering Akaike Information Criterion (AIC), and then by Likelihood Ratio Tests (LRTs) in case of nested models comparison [76]. All models which are considered for inclusion are reported in the Summary subsection of the respective dependent variable.
Results
Participant flow and recruitment
The flow of participants is detailed in the CONSORT diagram (S 1.3. Participant flow). Invitations for participation were sent in March 2023, the measurement phase was executed from May to June 2023.
Baseline data and study assumptions

We aimed to assess the differences between intervention sequences (ÉOS:Control and Control:ÉOS) and between sessions during non-intervention phases (baseline and post-MAST). We conducted rmANOVA tests with Bonferroni correction for variables measured at baseline and after MAST (Subjective stress, PA, and NA), and paired t-tests for baseline-only variables (KSS). Results showed no significant differences in baseline values between groups or sessions (S4. Study assumptions). Instances of violated normality assumptions are described in S4. as well. Descriptive statistics of baseline data by intervention, session, sex, and intervention sequence are described in S3.1.Questionnaires.

For physiological variables (rMSSD, LF, FAA, Theta/Beta FP1, and Theta/Beta FP2), measurements were taken during baseline, MAST instructions (ECG and EEG), and MAST performance (ECG only due to EEG noise). rmANOVA results did not reject the null hypothesis for any physiological variable concerning grouping. The only exception was FAA, which was lower in the second session during MAST instruction with a large effect size (generalized eta square = 0.36; [77]). Detailed rmANOVA results are in S4. Study assumptions, descriptive statistics of baseline data by period, by period and sex, and by sequence are in SS3.2. Physiological data.
Experiment results

To assess the effectiveness of the blue light and coherent breathing intervention compared to a neutral condition following induced stress, we conducted a series of analyses targeting positive and negative emotions, sleepiness, and subjective stress. Boxplots visualizing differences in post-relaxation subjective values for ÉOS and Control interventions within the first and second interventions are displayed in Fig 1. We employed LMEM where the physiological metrics were included as fixed factors along with intervention type and post-stress values of the given subjective metrics to examine their interrelationship with the outcomes of interest. Additionally, we constructed models with physiological metrics as dependent variables, which are all listed and described in S5.1.1.-S5.1.6. Baseline and post-stress phases are assumed to be without significant difference (see previous section Baseline data and study assumptions). The experimental phase starts with either the ÉOS or Control intervention. Our analysis uses the period after intervention as the reference level for testing changes between the two groups during all experimental phases.

blocks.text: Subjective stress

Subjective stress was log-transformed and modelled using LMEM. A model incorporating the post-stress task subjective stress score alongside intervention type, HRV, and EEG data without outliers revealed a significant effect of both intervention type and post-stress subjective stress, along with Theta/Beta FP1 (S5.2.1.7.). A simplified model involving only these predictors (SS5.2.1.8.) indicated that attribution to a control group increased post-relaxation subjective stress by 31.23% (CI 21.41% and 41.83%); each point increase in post-stress subjective stress led to an 8.39% rise in post-relaxation values (CI 6.88% and 15.45%; p < 0.001), and Theta/Beta FP1 decreased subjective stress by 1.43% with borderline significance (CI −3.11% and 0.071%; p = 0.061). However, because the normality of residuals was violated, we advise caution in interpreting these estimates, as they may be less precise (Table 1).

Positive affect

Positive affect, modelled without transformation, was analysed using a LMEM. The full model with the baseline positive affect on the data without EEG outliers unveiled a significant relationship with baseline positive affect, intervention type, and Theta/Beta FP2 (S5.2.2.2. and S5.2.2.3.). The full model using post-stress positive affect found a significant effect of positive affect and intervention type (S5.2.2.4.). A simplified analysis focusing solely on significant predictors (S5.2.2.5.) showed a decrease in post-relaxation positive affect by 0.73 (SE = 0.06, p < 0.001) points, while the control intervention decreased positive affect by 1.85 (SE = 0.54, p < 0.001) points (Table 2). However, because the normality of residuals was violated, we advise caution in interpreting these estimates, as they may be less precise.

Subjective sleepiness

Sleepiness was analysed utilizing a LMEM. Findings from the full model (S5.2.4.2.) revealed significant effect of intervention, baseline sleepiness, and HRV variables. A simpler model (S5.2.4.3.) utilizing only those significant predictors revealed a decrease in subjective sleepiness by 0.84 points (SE = 0.17, p < 0.001) compared to the control condition, and an increase by 0.59 points (SE = 0.07, p < 0.001) with each point in baseline sleepiness. Moreover, each ms2 of LF exhibited a positive association with sleepiness, increasing it by 0.0002 points (SE = 0.003, p = 0.002), whereas each ms of rMSSD was inversely related to sleepiness (p = 0.009), decreasing it by 0.009 points (SE = 0.003) per ms (Table 4). Normality of the models’ residuals was violated.

Discussion

Our results demonstrated that a 0.1 Hz coherent breathing intervention, guided by blue light, was more effective than a control condition in reducing subjective stress (−31.23%, CI 21.41% and 41.83%) and sleepiness (−0.84 points, SE = 0.17), and at promoting positive affect (1.85 points, SE = 0.54) after an episode of multisource acute stress in a workplace laboratory setting. However, there was no significant impact on negative affect. These findings partially support our hypothesis that the intervention would outperform the control condition [41] and suggest that this intervention can effectively enhance mood and reduce stress while preventing sleepiness after an episode of an acute stress.

This adds a novel perspective to previous studies. For instance, Minguillon et al. [20] did not find significant stress reduction differences in their study, perhaps due to their inclusion of blue light in both experimental sessions. Our results align with earlier findings on blue light’s positive effect on mood in controlled experiments with blue [78] or blue-enriched light [79,80], and its use in treating seasonal affective disorder [81], although the latter report non-uniform results. It should be noted that these types of exposures are recommended during daytime or complemented with sufficient daytime external light exposure when used at night [82] to prevent negative effects on circadian rhythm and sleep [83].

Regarding sleepiness, our intervention was effective in sleepiness reduction. This indicates that the intervention may effectively prevent the induction of sleepiness in post-stress relaxation measures. This mirrors findings from previous studies using blue light [23,25,84]. To our knowledge, there are no experimental studies on subjective sleepiness after coherent breathing interventions for direct comparison. Additionally, a meta-analysis on slow-paced breathing suggests there is no significant effect on subjective stress [85], with some studies even reporting negative effects on positive arousal [86]. Our results indicate that combining blue-light guidance with coherent breathing may offset these negative effects.

Another important finding is that, during the model selection phase, subjective measures taken post-stress had higher predictive power than baseline values (all models within the selection procedure are detailed in S5. Experimental phase modelling), highlighting the importance of individual reactivity to stress in determining the intervention’s effectiveness. This suggests that those more impacted by stress may benefit more from reactive countermeasures.

The lack of association between HRV and emotions or subjective stress in our study contrasts with extensive literature [85,87–89]. Notwithstanding, such a comparison is complicated due to the differences in study design, type of stimuli, and analyses conducted (detailed in reviews by Danilenko [90] and Katsuura and Lee [91]). However, we found a significant negative relationship with rMSSD and subjective sleepiness as well as a positive relationship with LF and subjective sleepiness, indicating evidence of physiological arousal coupling with subjective experience. Altogether, it seems like the specific combination of different stimuli introduces another level of interaction with potentially different effects than blue light and coherent breathing individually, which would deserve further investigation in a larger study.

As for the selected EEG variables of FAA and theta/beta ratios, our study identified significant but marginal effects of theta/beta ratio on negative affect. Inclusion of theta/beta ratios tended to improve the model’s performance, according to BIC criteria. Theta/beta ratio has been extensively linked to attention deficit and hyperactivity disorder [92,93]. Our results, thus, may suggest that individuals with hemispheric asymmetry in the theta/beta ratio may be more prone to express negative emotions. The lack of association of FAA with variables is in alignment with some previous studies which did not find an association between alpha asymmetry and stress response either [94,95]. However, other research found such evidence [96–98], suggesting the need of further investigation of this relationship.

Our study faced some limitations.  The normality of residuals was violated in all models.  This means there are possible prediction errors and reduced estimate precision [99], especially with a relatively small sample size compared to the number of predictors [76].  Our study also did not account for multiple hypotheses testing and has to be considered separately.  While a cross-over design enhances statistical power and estimate precision [47,100], some effects might remain undetected due to their smaller size or untested hidden factors.  Future studies should replicate our design with a larger, presumably more ethnically diverse population as there is some incidence that the effects may not be dependent on ethnic origin [101].  Another potential next step may involve the comparison of different light conditions (darkness, natural, and artificial light), and in more stratified grouping (coherent breathing without light guidance, or light without breathing modulation) to isolate and delineate the specific effects of each intervention type.

Assessing long-term effects of these in-office interventions and including cognitive tests post-intervention could further elucidate the practical impact of these stress countermeasures.  Notably, two recent studies further support these future directions.  Canazei et al.  [102] demonstrated that light-guided resonant breathing significantly enhanced autonomic recovery (RMSSD) following acute stress induction in a simulated office environment, corroborating our findings and underlining the potential of light-guided breathing as an occupational stress recovery strategy.  DeGraves et al.  [103] showed that coherent breathing is a feasible and effective stress management strategy for long-term care workers over an 8-week period, suggesting applicability beyond acute stress contexts.
Conclusion

In conclusion, our study demonstrates that a 0.1 Hz coherent breathing intervention, guided by blue light, effectively reduces subjective stress and sleepiness while promoting positive affect in a workplace laboratory setting. These findings align with and expand upon previous research, suggesting the potential for such interventions to provide short-term stress relief and mood enhancement without inducing sleepiness. The lack of association between HRV and emotional measures highlights the complexity of these interactions and the need for further investigation. Future research should explore the long-term effects of these interventions, their application across diverse populations, and their integration with other light and breathing modalities to enhance their effectiveness.

blocks.text: Abstract
Objectives

To evaluate the proof-of-concept feasibility of identifying individuals at high risk of cardiovascular disease through community-based PocDoc Healthy Heart point-of-care screening in a large, ethnically diverse, disadvantaged real-world cohort in the United Kingdom.
Methods

Proof-of-concept, non-randomised, non-interventional real-world cardiovascular disease risk case finding study in adults aged 18 years or older in real-world communities across the United Kingdom. Main outcome measures were identification of individuals with high risk of cardiovascular disease, defined as QRISK3 score ≥10%; and individuals meeting the criteria for weight loss, smoking cessation, or hypertension management services.
Results

A total of 4,256 individuals (mean age 49 years, 57% male, 31% body mass index ≥30 kg/m2) were included in the Primary Cohort. The Targeted Outreach and Workplace sub-cohorts comprised 1,970 and 756 individuals, respectively. In the Primary Cohort, 35% (1,486/4,256) had high (>5.0 mmol/L) total serum cholesterol, 10% were smokers, 10% met criteria for weight loss services and 19% met criteria for hypertension management services. QRISK3 scores were generated for individuals who had not previously had a cardiovascular disease event (~90% of screened individuals). A QRISK3 score ≥10% was found in 20% (784/3,842) of individuals in the Primary Cohort, 26% (457/1,743) in the Targeted Outreach sub-cohort, and 6% (41/701) in the Workplace sub-cohort. In the Primary Cohort, 60% (472/784) of individuals with a QRISK3 score ≥10% were not being treated with a lipid-lowering therapy at the time of testing.
Conclusions

In this proof-of-concept study, community-based point-of-care screening identified individuals with elevated cardiovascular risk and unmet cardiovascular risk management needs. These findings are hypothesis-generating and provide the rationale for further controlled studies with systematic follow-up and health-economic analyses to evaluate whether this approach can deliver improved clinical and system-level outcomes.
Trial registration
ClinicalTrials.gov NCT06258005
Introduction

Although cardiovascular disease (CVD) is a leading cause of death globally, most premature deaths caused by CVD are preventable by risk factor modification [1]. Dyslipidaemia, obesity, hypertension and diabetes are key modifiable risk factors for CVD and are targeted by preventative medicine initiatives such as the NHS Health Check (NHS-HC) in the United Kingdom (UK) [2,3]. The NHS-HC is a mandated national prevention programme in England that offers adults aged 40–74 years without pre-existing vascular disease a cardiovascular risk assessment every five years. The programme is delivered primarily through general practice and includes measurement of blood pressure (BP), lipid levels, body mass index (BMI), physical activity, alcohol consumption, smoking status, and family history, with QRISK2 or QRISK3 assessment to calculate a 10-year CVD risk. Individuals identified as high risk (≥10% 10-year CVD risk) are offered interventions including lifestyle advice, lipid-lowering therapy, and referral to specialist services. However, the NHS-HC programme currently only reaches a minority of those eligible for the programme and struggles to reach people in deprived parts of the UK, where the burden of CVD and comorbid conditions is the highest [4,5].

Barriers to NHS-HC CVD risk screening in the general population in England include lack of awareness or knowledge, competing priorities, including work commitments, and difficulty obtaining an appointment with a general practitioner (GP) [6]. Furthermore, because of pressures on primary care, some GP surgeries are not prioritising preventative healthcare compared to acute care appointments. Consequently, only 27% of eligible patients have had an NHS-HC in the past 5 years and uptake may be as low as 10% in some areas [7]. Targeted community and workplace screening initiatives may overcome some of these barriers, and identify individuals at high risk of CVD who are unaware of their risk [8].

Risk-factor modification interventions such as smoking cessation, weight loss management, diabetes and hypertension management, and lipid lowering therapy, are key strategies for reducing CVD risk among high-risk individuals [9]. Costs and the requirement for specialised equipment have limited the large-scale implementation of community CVD risk assessment, particularly where point-of-care lipid testing, an important component of CVD risk assessment, is included [10,11].

The PocDoc Healthy Heart Screen includes a digitally integrated point-of-care lipid-testing microfluidic device embedded within a cardiovascular screening application that uses the QRISK3 risk-prediction algorithm [12]. QRISK3 uses a combination of cardiovascular risk factors to estimate the risk of a CVD event within a ten year period. The UK’s NHS defines high risk as a QRISK3 score ≥10% [13]. This study evaluated the feasibility the PocDoc Healthy Heart device to identify individuals at high risk of CVD through point-of-care screening in a large, ethnically diverse, socioeconomically disadvantaged real-world cohort in the United Kingdom.

This proof-of-concept evaluation assessed whether community-based point-of-care screening could identify high-risk individuals outside traditional primary care pathways. It used a pragmatic, observational design that prioritised real-world feasibility over controlled experimental conditions. The findings should therefore be interpreted as hypothesis-generating rather than as an evaluation of comparative performance or system-level impact.
Methods

The primary aim of this community screening study (NCT06258005) was to identify individuals with a high risk of CVD, defined as having a QRISK3 score ≥10%, the threshold at which NICE Guideline NG238 recommends consideration of CVD risk reduction interventions following an informed discussion [9]. Additional aims included the estimation of proportions of screened individuals that could be eligible for referral to other NHS risk reduction programmes, regardless of QRISK3 score, including weight loss management, smoking cessation and hypertension management. Eligibility criteria of BMI > 30 kg/m2 for White and >27 kg/m2 for Asian/Black/ethnic minority people; and a diagnosis of diabetes, hypertension or both was used for weight loss management [14]. Smoking cessation eligibility criteria included any level of current tobacco smoking, and hypertension management eligibility criteria were BP reading recorded as 140/90 mm Hg or higher or 150/90 mm Hg or higher if aged >80 years (after repeat readings) [15].

Individuals from across the United Kingdom were included in the study (S1 Fig). Participants had access to approved mobile devices to run a PocDoc mobile application (app) either via private ownership or via community screening partners. Lifestyle and dietary recommendations, and referral to consult their GP were offered based on the PocDoc Healthy Heart screening results, with participants with one or more risk factors being offered advice (S1 Fig).
Study cohorts

The Primary Cohort included all participants who successfully completed the PocDoc screening procedure.  Two sub-cohorts were derived from the Primary Cohort: a Targeted Outreach Sub-Cohort, which included participants screened in community settings identified as being in areas with high levels of undiagnosed CVD risk; and a Workplace Sub-Cohort, which included participants screened at workplaces.  Participants screened outside the Targeted Outreach and Workplace cohorts were screened in pharmacy or home settings.  Screening locations were selected in collaboration with local health authorities (Health Innovation North-East and North Cumbria) and community partners (Howbeck Healthcare) to target areas with high levels of socioeconomic deprivation, low NHS-HC uptake, and ethnically diverse populations known to have elevated cardiovascular risk.  Individual-level socioeconomic status data was not systematically collected.  However, screening locations were purposefully selected in areas of high socioeconomic deprivation, particularly for the Targeted Outreach Sub-Cohort, to address health inequalities in cardiovascular screening access.

Targeted Outreach Sub-Cohort screening sites included shopping centres, leisure centres, places of worship (churches, mosques), football stadiums, women’s groups, foodbanks, asylum seeker forums, farmers’ markets, and Traveller events – venues with high footfall of individuals likely to face barriers to traditional primary care access.  Workplace Sub-Cohort screening was conducted at employer sites that agreed to offer screening to employees during working hours.  Home screening was offered to participants who self-referred through the PocDoc platform in partnership with local pharmacies.  Recruitment was passive, with participants voluntarily approaching screening stations at community events or requesting home testing.  No formal advertising campaigns or targeted invitations were used.  Healthcare professionals staffing screening events provided information about the screening programme and obtained consent from all participants.
Screening procedure

Screening using the PocDoc Healthy Heart device was conducted between June 23, 2023 and June 30, 2024 as described elsewhere and summarised in S2 and S3 Figs [12]. The digitally integrated PocDoc Healthy Heart test comprises a single-use microfluidic PocDoc lipid-panel assay, measurements of height, weight, and BP, and a medical questionnaire. The analytical performance of the PocDoc lipid panel has been previously validated against standard laboratory methods [12]. The device received regulatory clearance as a medical device under UK regulations (UKCA marking) and operates within the quality standards required for point-of-care testing in the UK. The Healthy Heart device includes a smartphone application that runs a full QRISK3 assessment using the acquired data. QRISK is used routinely in clinical practice to determine the risk of an individual suffering a cardiovascular event over the next decade [13,16]. PocDoc is the largest provider of QRISK3 scores in the UK outside of the NHS. For this study, a QRISK3 score ≥10% was treated as meeting the threshold for consideration of CVD risk-reduction interventions under NICE Guideline NG238. Separate prespecified criteria were used to identify participants for whom hypertension-management, weight-management, or smoking-cessation services could be considered [17,18].

BP measurement was an optional component of the screening protocol. Not all participants completed all screening components due to the pragmatic nature of the community-based testing, time constraints at screening events, equipment availability, or participant preference. QRISK3 scores could only be calculated for participants without prior CVD events and with sufficient data to complete the algorithm. The proportion of participants completing each screening component is reported in the Results section.
Ethics

The study was conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki, and all participants provided written informed consent. Ethics approval was granted under the Integrated Research Application System (IRAS number 325988).
Patient and public involvement
Patients and members of the public were not involved in the design, conduct, reporting, or dissemination of this research.
Statistical analysis

All analyses were descriptive. Categorical data are presented as counts and percentages, with the relevant analysis population as the denominator. Continuous data are summarized as the number of observations (n), mean and standard deviation (SD).
Measures to mitigate potential bias

Several authors (KR, KB, LD, SR) are employees and shareholders of the company developing the PocDoc device and application. To mitigate potential bias, the study was designed and conducted in collaboration with independent NHS organizations (Health Innovation North-East and North Cumbria, Howbeck Healthcare) who were involved in site selection, participant recruitment, and data collection. The study protocol was prospectively registered (NCT06258005) prior to data collection. Ethics approval was obtained from an independent NHS Research Ethics Committee (IRAS 325988). Raw data collection was performed by healthcare professionals employed by NHS partner organizations, not by company employees. The statistical analysis followed a pre-specified plan using only descriptive methods appropriate for the observational study design, thus minimizing opportunities for selective reporting or data manipulation. Notwithstanding these measures, the involvement of commercial co-authors in manuscript preparation represents an inherent limitation that readers should consider when interpreting the findings.
Results
Screening cohorts

The total number of participants approached or the denominator population eligible for screening was not systematically collected across screening venues, limiting our ability to calculate formal uptake rates. This absence of uptake denominators means that observed proportions of high-risk participants reflect the characteristics of those who self-selected to participate and cannot be generalised to the wider populations of the screening locations. Participation was entirely voluntary, with participants self-selecting to attend community screening events. The characteristics of those who participated (Table 1) may differ from non-participants in unmeasured ways. The Targeted Outreach Sub-Cohort included high representation of ethnic minorities (47% Non-White vs. 26% in the Primary Cohort) and high rates of previous CVD events (6% vs. 2% in the Workplace Sub-Cohort), suggesting engagement with high-risk communities. However, we cannot determine whether those who declined screening or did not attend events differ systematically in cardiovascular risk profile from those who participated.

Because of the community nature of the screening, equipment limitations and individual’s preferences, some data fields were not collected for some participants. BP measurements were taken for only 63% of participants in the Primary Cohort. Lipid levels were measured successfully for all participants. Sufficient data was obtained for QRISK3 measurement in 90% of participants. These missing data mean that estimates of hypertension prevalence and cardiovascular risk are based on incomplete samples and may not be representative of the full screened population.

Participants in the Primary Cohort (N = 4,256) had a mean age of 49 years; were 57% male; and most were overweight or obese. Only 29% of the Primary Cohort participants stated they had had a health check including a lipid panel in the past five years, 45% reported they had not, and 26% did not answer the question (Table 1). Compared with the Workplace Sub-Cohort (N = 756), the Targeted Outreach Sub-Cohort (N = 1,970) was more ethnically diverse, older, had higher BMI, had had fewer prior cholesterol checks, had more prevalent history of CVD and had a higher proportion of current smokers (Table 1). These baseline differences between sub-cohorts preclude any meaningful direct comparison of QRISK3 or risk factor rates across cohorts.
Identification of participants with high total cholesterol, HDL cholesterol, non-HDL cholesterol and triglycerides

Serum total cholesterol, HDL cholesterol, non-HDL cholesterol, and triglycerides were quantified in 4,256 participants in the Primary Cohort, in 1,970 in the Targeted Outreach Sub-Cohort and in 756 in the Workplace Sub-Cohort (Table 2). In the Primary Cohort, 35% had total serum cholesterol levels ≥5 mmol/L; 21% had serum non-HDL ≥ 4 mmol/L; 25% had HDL ≤ 1.0 mmol/L for males/ ≤ 1.2 mmol/L for females; 27% had triglycerides ≥2.3 mmol/L; and 20% had a triglyceride:HDL ratio ≥4 (Fig 1). Similar patterns were observed in the Targeted Outreach and Workplace Sub-Cohorts, though these descriptive observations should be interpreted considering the baseline differences between cohorts noted above.

blocks.text: Identification of participants with potential hypertension

At screening, 3,550/4,256 (83%) participants stated that they were not taking any antihypertensive medication, and 706 (17%) stated that they were on antihypertensive treatment. BP data from 2,671/4,256 (63%) participants in the Primary Cohort were available for inclusion in the CVD risk assessment. As BP data were missing for 37% of the Primary Cohort, the following estimates are based on those who provided BP readings and may not be representative of the full screened cohort.

A total of 810/2,671 (30%) had BP readings above the normal range (i.e., systolic BP > 140 mm Hg or diastolic BP > 90 mm Hg if aged 80 years or younger; 150/90 or higher if aged >80 years), including 610/2,671 (23%) that were not on any antihypertensive treatment. Additionally, among the 474 participants that were on antihypertensive treatment and that provided their BP, 210/474 (44%) had BP above the recommended range.
Identification of participants meeting prespecified criteria for consideration of existing preventative care programmes

QRISK3 scores were generated for participants who had not previously had a CVD event, which was approximately 90% of all screened participants (Table 3). A total of 20% (784/3,842) of participants in the Primary Cohort, 26% (457/1,743) in the Targeted Outreach Sub-Cohort, and 6% (41/701) in the Workplace Sub-Cohort had a QRISK3 score ≥10% (i.e., a ≥ 10% or greater risk of developing CVD within 10 years) making them eligible for consideration for CVD risk reduction in line with NICE Guideline 238 (Table 3) [9]. The observed variation in QRISK3 scores ≥10% between cohorts (26% in Targeted Outreach vs. 20% in Primary vs. 6% in Workplace) reflects differences in the underlying characteristics of populations accessing these different screening settings (Table 1), rather than representing a controlled comparison of screening effectiveness.

The proportion of screened participants meeting criteria for consideration for smoking cessation or weight loss management services was 10% across the Primary Cohort whilst 19% of all screened participants were eligible to be considered for hypertension management (Table 3).

In the Primary Cohort, 60% (472/784) of the screened participants with a QRISK3 score ≥10% were not being treated with a lipid-lowering therapy such as a statin. Only 44% of these participants at high-risk of CVD events had previously had a health check including a full lipid panel.
Referral of participants to onward care pathways

The PocDoc Healthy Heart questionnaire included an optional field that asked whether lifestyle or dietary advice was provided to the person being screened, or whether the person was recommended to visit their GP for follow-up care. A total of 1,714 (75%) of participants answering the question were given lifestyle and/or dietary advice following their PocDoc screen, and 760 (33%) of participants were recommended to visit their GP for follow-up care (Table 3). Whether participants acted on these recommendations was not captured in this study, and referral rates should therefore be interpreted as guidance given rather than confirmed follow-up.
User experience

Participants in the Primary Cohort and the Targeted Outreach and Workplace Sub-Cohorts reported high likelihoods of recommending the PocDoc test to a family member (Net Promoter Scores of 88, 93 and 90, respectively; S1 Table), and 93% of participants found the PocDoc test more convenient that being tested at a GP surgery (S2 Table). These user experience data reflect self-reported perceptions of acceptability and convenience, and do not constitute evidence of clinical effectiveness or superiority over existing care pathways.
Discussion

This proof-of-concept study found that community-based point-of-care cardiovascular screening using the PocDoc Healthy Heart device was feasible in the settings studied and can identify participants with elevated CVD risk who had not been previously screened. Over four thousand people participated in the study, with approximately one in five participants having a QRISK score of ≥10% and therefore being at high risk of having a CVD event within the next ten years. The majority of these participants (60%) were not receiving lipid lowering therapy at the time of screening. However, these descriptive findings do not establish clinical benefit or comparative performance against existing screening pathways.

Outreach community screening was conducted in shopping centres, leisure centres, churches, mosques, football stadiums, women’s groups, foodbanks, asylum-seeker forums, farmers’ markets and Traveller events. In this Targeted Outreach Sub-Cohort, which comprised older, more ethnically diverse individuals with high comorbidity levels (Table 1), one in four people for whom a QRISK3 score was calculated had a QRISK3 score of ≥10%. This finding demonstrates that the screening was able to identify people at high risk of CVD. However, it also reflects the characteristics of the self-selected population attending these venues and cannot directly be interpreted as evidence that community screening is more effective than existing pathways, or that it would yield similar rates in other populations or settings. Given the substantial baseline differences between cohorts (Table 1), direct comparisons between screening settings would not be appropriate without statistical adjustment and were not performed in this proof-of-concept study.

Among participants with a QRISK3 score of ≥10%, one in four met the recorded criteria for consideration of hypertension management, six in ten were not receiving lipid-lowering therapy, and eight in ten had a BMI in the overweight or obese range. The study did not assess whether screening recommendations led to treatment initiation, engagement with services, or reduction in CVD risk. These outcomes require prospective evaluation with appropriate comparators and follow-up.

In the Primary Cohort, 813 participants had BP above the prespecified threshold which made them eligible for the hypertension management service; this represented 30% of those with recorded BP and 19% of the full cohort. Among participants who reported antihypertensive treatment and had recorded BP, 44% had a reading above the prespecified treatment target threshold. However, only 63% of the Primary Cohort provided BP readings, and findings may therefore not represent the full screened population. Observations are descriptive and hypothesis-generating; future studies with complete BP data and appropriate controls are needed to determine whether community screening adds value over existing pathways in managing hypertension at the population level. A high proportion of screened participants were eligible for other existing preventative care pathways including weight management and smoking cessation. Although some participants received recommendations to consult their GP, the study did not record whether they attended primary care or engaged with onward services, and no clinical impact can therefore be inferred.

The findings from our study are consistent with previous community reports that community pharmacy and workplace programmes can identify high-risk individuals and improve access to screening outside of primary care [19–30]. The NHS-HC programme has also been delivered in community venues, with pilot studies reporting reach into some underserved groups [31,32]. The present study adds descriptive evidence that integrated point-of-care lipid testing and comprehensive QRISK3 assessment can be delivered across diverse community settings including non-traditional venues such as places of worship, foodbanks, and asylum-seeker forums. In the Primary Cohort, 45% reported no health check in the previous five years, 29% reported such a check and 26% did not answer the question. This pattern suggests that community screening may engage some people without recent lipid testing, but the absence of uptake denominators and self-selected sampling preclude conclusions about population reach and comparative performance. Questions about subsequent adherence, costs and effects on health inequalities also remain [21].

The PocDoc Healthy Heart screen uses a smartphone camera to quantify enzymatic colorimetric reactions from a point-of-care lipid panel in a microfluidic assay, and integrates lipid results alongside other screen-derived measurements including height, weight, BP and medical history to estimate a person’s ten-year CVD risk score (QRISK score) and their healthy heart age [12]. QRISK3 estimates a person’s risk of myocardial infarction (MI) or stroke over a 10-year period and was derived using data from over ten million UK primary care patients [13]. Under NICE Guideline NG238, a risk score of ≥10% is the threshold for offering atorvastatin for primary prevention after an informed discussion of risks and benefits [9].

The implications of community screening for primary care workload requires careful consideration. In this study, 33% of screened participants (760/2,283 responding) were recommended to consult their GP for follow-up care. Acting upon these recommendations could generate additional appointments. However, the study did not record subsequent GP attendance or healthcare utilization and therefore cannot determine the direction or magnitude of any effect on workload.

Early identification of cardiovascular risk could, in principle, facilitate preventive management and potentially reduce acute presentations. However, this study did not assess whether identified risks would have otherwise remained undetected, whether recommended care was initiated or whether acute cardiovascular events were prevented. Any effect on subsequent emergency presentations remains hypothetical.

Electronic transmission of screening results directly to GP records (introduced in the PocDoc application after this study’s conclusion) may reduce reliance on participant-initiated communication but its effect on workflow has not been evaluated here. The balance between prevention workload and averted acute care resource use should be evaluated in future cost-effectiveness and healthcare utilization studies. For the 60% of high-risk participants not on lipid-lowering therapy, initiating statins represents a straightforward, evidence-based intervention that could be delivered efficiently in primary care.
Limitations of study

This proof-of-concept, real-world study has several limitations.  First, missing data for key variables reflects the pragmatic nature of community screening; for example, BP measurements were available for only 63% of the Primary Cohort.  Missing data arose from time constraints at community events, equipment availability, participant preference to decline certain measurements, and the optional nature of some screening components.  These missing data may introduce selection bias if participants declining measurements differ systematically from those completing the full assessment.  Second, potential language barriers may have limited minority group engagement despite targeting ethnically diverse communities.  Third, the study relied on participants pursuing referrals to consult their GP if identified as having high CVD risk, with no systematic follow-up to confirm whether referrals were completed.  After this study concluded, changes have been made to the PocDoc screening process to enable GPs to receive results directly to overcome this limitation.

Fourth, as a proof-of-concept observational study without a control group, we cannot assess the comparative effectiveness of community screening versus standard NHS Health Check delivery, nor can we evaluate long-term clinical outcomes or cost-effectiveness.  The absence of systematic data on screening uptake rates represents a limitation in interpreting the reach and potential selection bias of community screening.  Those who voluntarily participated in community screening may differ from non-participants in health awareness, health-seeking behaviour, perceived risk, or actual cardiovascular risk burden.  This self-selection may lead to either overestimation (if worried participants with symptoms participated preferentially) or underestimation (if healthy participants took part out of curiosity while those with known problems avoided screening) of true community CVD risk prevalence.  Future implementation should include systematic capture of uptake rates to better understand reach and representativeness.

Finally, the involvement of commercial co-investigators in the study design and manuscript preparation, despite the mitigation measures described, may have influenced study conduct or reporting in ways that are difficult to quantify.  Readers should weigh these potential sources of bias when interpreting the findings.
Priorities for future research

Although individual socio-economic status (SES) data were unavailable for analysis, our targeted approach, i.e., screening in deprived communities, places of worship, foodbanks, and asylum seeker forums, to reach high-risk, underserved groups (Table 1), may support the feasibility of community screening to address access inequalities. Future implementation studies will integrate individual SES measures and longitudinal follow-up to quantify equity impacts using validated metrics (e.g., proportion screened by deprivation quintile, uptake by ethnicity).

Cost-effectiveness analysis was beyond the scope of this proof-of-concept feasibility study and represents an important direction for future research. Preliminary cost considerations suggest that community-based screening may offer potential advantages through reduced primary care facility overhead, batch processing of multiple participants at community events, and reaching populations with low NHS-HC uptake who would otherwise not be screened. However, comprehensive cost-effectiveness evaluation would need to account for equipment costs, healthcare professional time, consumables, referral management, downstream healthcare utilization following identification of high-risk individuals, and most importantly, long-term clinical outcomes including cardiovascular events prevented. Such analyses should be a priority for future studies before widespread implementation can be recommended. A separate economic evaluation of this programme is currently under review and will further address these questions, but detailed cost-effectiveness findings are beyond the scope of the present article.

The NHS-HC initiative is a national risk assessment and management programme that is free at point-of-care for adults aged 40–74 years living in England who do not currently have any vascular disorders and are not being treated for risk factors such as diabetes [33]. However, the uptake of NHS-HC has been poor, with only 27% of eligible participants having had an NHS-HC in the past five years. In some areas this may be as low as 10% [7].

Based on the findings and limitations of this proof-of-concept study, we propose several areas of development for community-based cardiovascular screening programs.  First, systematic capture of uptake rates and participation demographics is essential to evaluate reach and identify under-represented groups.  Second, direct electronic transmission of results to GP practices should be standard to ensure continuity of care and reduce reliance on patient-initiated follow-up.  Third, integration with existing NHS prevention pathways is critical, including pre-arranged referral protocols for weight management, smoking cessation, and hypertension services.  Fourth, community screening should target areas with documented low NHS Health Check uptake using local health intelligence to maximize impact on health inequalities.  Fifth, standardized training for healthcare professionals delivering community screening ensures consistent quality and appropriate management of results requiring urgent attention.  Sixth, partnerships with community organizations (faith groups, community centres, employers) facilitate access to target populations and build trust.

Seventh, multi-language materials and culturally competent staff are necessary to maximize engagement with ethnically diverse communities.  Finally, formal evaluation frameworks should be embedded from the outset, including long-term follow-up of cardiovascular events, treatment initiation and adherence, cost-effectiveness, and patient-reported outcomes.  Such a framework will ultimately support the sustainable delivery of community-based point-of-care testing as a complement to traditional primary care screening.
Conclusion

This proof-of-concept study found that community-based point-of-care cardiovascular screening using the PocDoc Healthy Heart device was feasible across the real-world settings studied. Individuals with elevated QRISK3 scores and unmet cardiovascular risk management needs were identified through the screens. A substantial proportion of those screened had not previously received a health check, suggesting that community screening may reach individuals with limited prior engagement with preventive services. These findings are descriptive and hypothesis-generating. Controlled studies with uptake denominators, systematic follow-up, appropriate comparators and health-economic evaluation are needed to determine the clinical outcomes, equity of reach and implications for health-service use.

The dataset contains potentially identifying patient health information collected under NHS Research Ethics Committee approval (IRAS 325988) with participant consent for use in this specific study. Under the terms of the ethical approval and participant consent, individual-level data cannot be made publicly available. Reasonable requests for access to anonymized aggregate data should be directed to the Robin Matthews (robin@mypocdoc.com) and Vital Signs Solutions for consideration by the study Data Access Committee, which will review requests in accordance with ethical and legal requirements. Requests will be assessed based on scientific merit, ethical appropriateness, and compliance with data protection regulations.
