blocks.text: Technological dimension. The technological context of the TOE framework concerns the technological capabilities and conditions that enable enterprises to adopt and develop new technologies. As a general-purpose technology, AI relies heavily on continuous knowledge accumulation and sustained R&D capability [43]. Compared with conventional technologies, AI-related R&D is characterized by greater complexity and path dependence, requiring repeated algorithm optimization, model iteration, and long-term technological investment [29]. Under binding energy constraints, enterprises may find it difficult to sustain computing-intensive activities, thereby restricting technological innovation [44]. Previous research shows that improvements in energy supply can reduce uncertainty surrounding R&D activities and improve the predictability of innovation investment, thereby supporting innovation output [45]. By improving power supply stability and reducing the risk of interruptions and voltage fluctuations, UHV transmission projects provide more reliable infrastructure conditions for sustained R&D activities [46]. These improvements can strengthen enterprises’ technological innovation capability and provide a stronger technological foundation for the AI development and application.

Organizational dimension. The organizational context of the TOE framework reflects the internal resources and capabilities that determine whether enterprises can effectively adopt emerging technologies. AI development requires substantial initial and continuing investment in computing infrastructure, data resources, specialized personnel, and related organizational capabilities [32]. Consequently, enterprises with limited internal resources may be less able to transform favorable technological conditions into actual AI development. UHV transmission projects can improve enterprises’ operating conditions by reducing energy-related costs and stabilizing electricity supply [11]. More reliable electricity supply reduces production disruptions and the associated operating losses, thereby preserving internal resources that can be allocated to R&D and technological capability building [47,48]. Therefore, UHV transmission projects can strengthen enterprises’ organizational capacity to undertake AI development by relaxing internal resource constraints.

Environmental dimension. The environmental context of the TOE framework concerns the external conditions that shape enterprises’ technology adoption and resource acquisition. For AI development, external financing conditions are particularly important because AI-related investment is capital-intensive, long-term, and subject to considerable uncertainty. Therefore, enterprises often require sustained access to external capital in addition to internally generated resources [49,50]. A more developed regional financial system can reduce financing frictions, improve capital allocation efficiency, and facilitate enterprises’ access to long-term funding for innovation and digital transformation [51,52]. By improving cross-regional energy allocation and electricity supply conditions, UHV transmission projects can support regional production and investment activities. More broadly, infrastructure improvements can facilitate resource flows and financial agglomeration, thereby creating more favorable conditions for regional financial development [53]. Improved regional financial development can then enhance enterprises’ access to stable external funding for AI-related R&D, computing investment, and technology deployment, thereby promoting their AI development.
Based on the above analysis, we propose the following hypotheses:
Hypothesis 2a. UHV transmission projects promote enterprises’ AI development by strengthening enterprises’ technological innovation capability.
Hypothesis 2b. UHV transmission projects promote enterprises’ AI development by expanding enterprises’ internal organizational resources.
Hypothesis 2c. UHV transmission projects promote enterprises’ AI development by improving regional financial development.
3. Methodology
3.1. Model setting

Using panel data of Chinese listed enterprises from 2007–2023, we treat the staggered rollout of UHV transmission projects across prefecture-level cities as a quasi-natural experiment to estimate their effect on enterprises’ AI development. For each city, we identify the year when it first gained access to the UHV network. Enterprises located in cities connected to UHV transmission projects are assigned to the treatment group from the corresponding year onward, while enterprises in cities without UHV access constitute the control group. To avoid capturing partial-year effects, UHV access occurring between July and December is treated as effective in the following year. Given the phased construction and staggered operation of UHV transmission projects across cities, this setting provides an appropriate framework for DID estimation. This identification strategy has been extensively applied in evaluating infrastructure and policy impacts [54,55].

The treatment variable is defined at the prefecture-city level because the effects of UHV transmission projects are realized through regional power systems rather than directly targeting individual enterprises. Therefore, the connection of a city to the UHV network represents an exogenous change in the external electricity supply environment faced by local enterprises. Based on this identification strategy, we construct the following baseline model:
AIit=β0+β1UHVit+βmControlsit+Yeart+Companyi+ℇit (1)

where i denotes enterprises and t denotes years. AI denotes enterprises’ AI development. UHV denotes the dummy variable of energy infrastructure construction. Controls denotes a set of control variables at the enterprise and city levels. Year and Company denote the year and enterprise fixed effects, respectively. ℇit denotes the random error term. Standard errors are clustered at the city level to address potential issues of serial correlation.
3.2. Variable definitions

Explained variable (AI). Following prior studies that use corporate disclosures to capture enterprises’ engagement with AI [56–58], we construct a text-based measure of enterprises’ AI development from their annual reports. Specifically, we compile an expanded dictionary of AI-related terms and count the total number of occurrences of these keywords in each firm-year annual report. Because the resulting count variable is highly right-skewed and contains zero values, we define AI as the natural logarithm of one plus the total keyword frequency. Annual reports contain information on enterprises’ strategic priorities, technological activities, and operating plans, making textual disclosures useful for identifying their engagement with emerging technologies. Compared with patent-based measures, the textual indicator can also capture AI-related activities at an earlier stage, before they are reflected in observable patent outcomes. Nevertheless, as textual measures may be affected by differences in disclosure intensity and report content, we conduct additional robustness tests using alternative specifications of the AI indicator.

Key explanatory variable (UHV). We use official records from the National Energy Administration, State Grid Corporation of China, and China Southern Power Grid to identify the commissioning date and route of each UHV transmission line. A firm-year is coded as 1 from the year its region first gains access to the UHV network onward, and 0 otherwise. In defining UHV access, we distinguish between DC and AC lines because their spatial transmission structures differ. DC lines are typically point-to-point without intermediate nodes, so the endpoint regions are treated as beneficiaries. AC lines may include intermediate substations, and regions along the route with such substations are therefore also classified as beneficiaries. This approach better matches the spatial and technical features of UHV transmission projects and helps identify where electricity supply conditions are likely to improve in practice [59].

Control variables. Referring to existing studies [60], we incorporate a series of firm-level and city-level control variables to mitigate potential omitted variable bias. Firm-level controls include: enterprise size (Size), the natural logarithm of operating revenue; enterprise age (Age), the natural logarithm of years since listing; cash flow (CF), the proportion of net cash flow from operating activities in total assets; fixed assets intensity (Far), the proportion of net fixed assets in total assets; growth (Growth), annual revenue growth rate; board size (Board), the natural logarithm of directors; ownership concentration (Top1), shareholding of the largest shareholder; female director ratio (Female), the proportion of female directors in the total number of board directors; and audit opinion (Opinion), a dummy that equals 1 for enterprise receiving a standard unqualified audit opinion and 0 otherwise. City-level controls include: fiscal self-sufficiency rate (Finance), the proportion of local general budgetary revenue in local general budgetary expenditure; and science and technology development level (Tech), the proportion of science and technology expenditure in local general budgetary expenditure.
3.3. Data and descriptive statistics

The empirical analysis draws on the panel data of Chinese A-share listed enterprises from 2007 to 2023. Annual reports are retrieved from Sina Finance platform. Firm-level financial data and basic corporate information are sourced from the China Stock Market & Accounting Research (CSMAR) Database and the China Research Data Services (CNRDS) Platform. City-level data are obtained from the China Statistical Yearbook.

Sample construction follows the procedures below. First, financial and insurance enterprises are excluded, as their balance sheets are different in nature and the comparability of innovation activities is limited. Second, eliminate the enterprises that are designated as ST or *ST during the sample period. Third, observations with missing values for core variables are removed from the dataset. Finally, to limit the interference of extreme values, all continuous variables are winsorized at the 1% and 99% percentiles within each year. To guarantee data integrity and structural consistency, we apply linear interpolation when necessary. Descriptive statistics for the main variables are reported in Table 1.

4. Empirical results
4.1. Baseline results

Table 2 presents the baseline regression results of Model (1). Column (1) includes only the UHV indicator, whose coefficient is positive and significant at the 1% level. Columns (2) to (4) sequentially add corporate financial controls, corporate governance controls, and city-level controls. The UHV coefficient remains significantly positive and statistically significant across all specifications, indicating that the association between UHV access and enterprises’ AI development is not driven by these observable firm- or city-level characteristics.

In Column (4), the estimated coefficient of UHV is 0.098, indicating an economically meaningful improvement in enterprises’ AI development following UHV access. More broadly, this result suggests that AI development depends not only on enterprises’ internal capabilities and policy support, but also on the infrastructure conditions under which enterprises operate. By strengthening cross-regional power transmission, UHV transmission projects may provide a more supportive energy environment for enterprises to undertake electricity- and computing-intensive AI activities. Overall, the baseline results provide strong statistical and economic support for Hypothesis 1.
4.2. Parallel trend test

A key prerequisite for identifying the treatment effect using a multi-period DID model is the parallel trends assumption [61]. Considering the relatively limited sample support at event times distant from policy implementation, we set the event-study window to five years before and after UHV access, with the year immediately preceding treatment serving as the reference period following prior research [62]. This window provides a sufficiently long pre-treatment period for assessing trend comparability while allowing the dynamic post-treatment effects to be captured.

As shown in Fig 2, the estimated coefficients in the pre-treatment periods remain close to zero and are statistically indistinguishable from zero. A further joint significance test fails to reject the null hypothesis that all pre-treatment coefficients are jointly equal to zero (p = 0.1386). This suggests that there is no significant systematic difference in the pre-treatment trends of AI development between firms in the treatment and control groups prior to UHV access, providing empirical support for the parallel trends assumption.
Fig 2. Parallel trend test results.
blocks.imageAlt: Fig 2 Parallel trend test results.

blocks.text: Following UHV access, the estimated coefficients become positive and exhibit a generally increasing pattern over time, indicating that the effect of UHV transmission projects on enterprises’ AI development is persistent and cumulative. The treatment effect does not fully materialize immediately after UHV access but becomes stronger in subsequent periods. One possible explanation is that improvements in electricity infrastructure require time to translate into innovation outcomes through adjustments in computing-resource allocation, digital investment, and R&D activities. Therefore, the innovation-enhancing effect of improved electricity infrastructure may be gradually realized over time. Overall, these findings not only provide empirical support for the parallel trends assumption underlying the DID model but also reveal the dynamic nature of the effect of UHV transmission projects on enterprises’ AI development.
4.3. Placebo test

To assess whether the baseline results are driven by unobserved confounders, omitted variables, or other concurrent factors, we conduct a placebo test following Autor and Dorn [63]. Specifically, we randomly assign a UHV commissioning year to each sample city and construct a placebo treatment indicator (UHV_false). We then re-estimate the baseline specification 1,000 times using the randomly assigned treatment and obtain the corresponding distributions of the estimated coefficients and P-values. Under a valid identification strategy, the coefficients generated from these placebo treatments should be concentrated around zero and exhibit little systematic statistical significance. Fig 3 reports the results.
Fig 3. Placebo test results.
blocks.imageAlt: Fig 3 Placebo test results.

blocks.text: The placebo coefficients are largely concentrated around zero, and most estimates are statistically insignificant. In contrast, the baseline coefficient of 0.098 lies in the right tail of the placebo distribution and is substantially larger than most simulated estimates. These findings suggest that the baseline effect is unlikely to be explained by random treatment assignment or other unobserved factors. Instead, the estimated effect is more likely to reflect systematic changes associated with access to UHV transmission projects rather than incidental variations across cities and years. Overall, the placebo test provides further support for the robustness of the baseline results.
4.4. Robustness checks
4.4.1. Instrumental variable strategy.

To address potential endogeneity arising from the non-random placement of UHV transmission projects, we further apply an IV approach to retest Hypothesis 1. Following Chen and Cheng [2], we use the interaction between the logarithm of the number of national nature reserves in each province and the post-operation indicator (Protect×Post) as the instrument. On the one hand, the instrument satisfies correlation, as the UHV routes are deliberately planned to bypass national nature reserves during the site selection process. On the other hand, it satisfies exogenousness, as natural reserves are areas designated by law for special protection and management, and do not directly affect enterprises’ AI development.

Table 3 reports the two-stage least squares (2SLS) results. The first-stage estimate in Column (1) shows a significant relationship between the instrument and UHV transmission projects. The Kleibergen-Paap Wald rk F statistic is 196.19, well above the Stock-Yogo critical value of 16.38, indicating strong instrument relevance. In the second stage in Column (2), the coefficient of UHV remains significantly positive at the 5% level. The Kleibergen-Paap rk LM statistic is 21.43 (p = 0.000), rejecting under-identification. These results suggest that the positive effect of UHV transmission projects is unlikely to be driven solely by endogenous project placement. More broadly, they indicate that the role of UHV transmission projects in enterprises’ AI development is not merely a reflection of projects being located in regions already better positioned for AI adoption, but is associated with the change in external infrastructure conditions itself. Therefore, the main conclusion remains robust.

4.4.2. Propensity score matching.

To reduce potential selection bias, we employ a propensity score matching and difference-in-differences (PSM-DID) approach. Specifically, Size, Age, CF, Board, Top1, Female, and Opinion in Model (1) are used as matching covariates, and UHV serves as the treatment indicator. The sample enterprises in the treatment group and in the control group are matched at a ratio of 1:2. After matching, the absolute standardized biases of all covariates fall below 10%, indicating satisfactory balance between the two groups. Column (1) of Table 4 reports the baseline regression results after sample matching. The coefficient of UHV remains significantly positive at the 1% level. This result suggests that the baseline effect is not primarily driven by systematic differences in observable characteristics between treated and untreated enterprises. It also strengthens the interpretation that the observed change in AI development is associated with UHV access rather than pre-existing sample composition.

4.4.3. Alternative dependent variable.

Text-based measures based on raw keyword counts may be affected by differences in annual-report length, as longer reports mechanically provide more opportunities for AI-related terms to appear. To mitigate this concern, following Mishra et al. [56], we normalize the frequency of AI-related keywords by the total number of words in each annual report and construct AI_Intensity, measured as the number of AI-related keywords per 10,000 words. This specification captures the relative intensity of AI-related disclosure rather than its absolute frequency. Column (2) of Table 4 shows that the coefficient of UHV remains significantly positive, indicating that the baseline result is not driven by differences in report length or disclosure verbosity.

We further address the possibility that AI-related terms appearing in other sections of annual reports may reflect general disclosure rather than firm-specific technological activities. The Management Discussion and Analysis (MD&A) section contains management’s discussion of operating conditions and forward-looking information and has been widely used in textual research to extract economically meaningful firm-level information [64]. We therefore reconstruct the dependent variable using only the MD&A section and define AI_MD&A as the natural logarithm of one plus the frequency of AI-related keywords in this section. Column (3) of Table 4 shows that the coefficient of UHV remains significantly positive. Because the MD&A provides a more focused account of enterprises’ operations and future plans, the persistence of the UHV effect under this narrower textual measure reduces the concern that the baseline finding is driven by AI-related language appearing in less relevant sections of annual reports.

Taken together, these two alternative measures address different sources of potential measurement error in the text-based AI indicator. Normalizing by report length mitigates mechanical differences arising from disclosure volume, while restricting the analysis to the MD&A reduces noise from less relevant sections of annual reports. The consistent results provide stronger evidence that the baseline AI measure captures variation in enterprises’ AI-related strategic and technological engagement rather than merely differences in reporting style or document structure.
4.4.4. Excluding concurrent policies.

Several national policies implemented during the sample period may also affect enterprises’ AI development. To account for these concurrent policy shocks, we further control for three major initiatives. First, we consider the National Big Data Comprehensive Pilot Zone (NBDPZ) policy, which was launched in 2015 and subsequently expanded in batches, and construct DID1 accordingly (Table 5, Column (1)). Second, we control for the Broadband China (BC) policy, introduced in 2013 and gradually extended to additional pilot cities during 2014–2016, using DID2 (Table 5 Column (2)). Third, we consider the National Artificial Intelligence Innovation and Development Pilot Zone (NAIPZ) policy, implemented in three batches between 2019 and 2021, and construct DID3 (Table 5, Column (3)). Each indicator equals 1 from the year in which the corresponding policy was implemented in the enterprise’s city and 0 otherwise.

4.5. Heterogeneity analyses

The effect of UHV transmission projects on enterprises’ AI development may vary with enterprises’ initial constraints and their capacity to convert improved infrastructure conditions into technology investment. On the one hand, the marginal value of electricity infrastructure is likely to be greater for enterprises facing stronger resource or infrastructure constraints, because improvements in electricity availability can relax previously binding limitations. On the other hand, the extent to which these benefits translate into AI development depends on enterprises’ organizational responsiveness and technological absorptive capacity. Accordingly, we examine heterogeneity along four dimensions: ownership, regional location, corporate governance structure, and technological intensity. The first two dimensions capture differences in pre-existing constraints, whereas the latter two reflect differences in enterprises’ ability to respond to and utilize improved infrastructure conditions.
4.5.1. Ownership type.

Ownership differences may shape enterprises’ exposure to external resource constraints. Compared with state-owned enterprises (SOEs), non-SOEs generally have weaker access to financing and other strategic resources, making long-term and uncertain AI investment more sensitive to changes in operating conditions. Therefore, improvements in electricity availability and reliability may generate greater marginal benefits for non-SOEs, whereas stronger resource access may reduce SOEs’ responsiveness to the same infrastructure improvement. We thus expect the effect of UHV transmission projects on AI development to be stronger for non-SOEs.

To test this expectation, we construct a binary indicator (SOE), which equals 1 for SOEs and 0 for non-SOEs, and divide the sample accordingly. Columns (1)-(2) of Table 7 show that the coefficients of UHV are positive in both groups, but statistically significant only for non-SOEs. The coefficient difference test further confirms that the effect is significantly larger for non-SOEs. This finding suggests that energy infrastructure generates greater marginal value for enterprises facing stronger initial resource constraints.

4.5.2. Regional heterogeneity.

The marginal value of infrastructure improvement may also depend on existing regional infrastructure conditions. Coastal regions generally have more developed infrastructure, factor markets, and innovation ecosystems, leaving relatively less room for additional energy infrastructure to relax existing constraints. In contrast, enterprises in inland regions are more likely to face limitations in infrastructure accessibility and factor allocation, making improvements in electricity supply particularly valuable for electricity- and computing-intensive activities. Therefore, we expect the effect of UHV transmission projects on enterprises’ AI development to be stronger in inland regions.

To examine regional differences, we construct a binary indicator (Coastal), which equals 1 for enterprises located in coastal regions and 0 for those in inland regions. Columns (3)-(4) of Table 7 show that the coefficients of UHV are positive in both groups, but statistically significant only for inland enterprises. The coefficient difference test confirms that the effect is significantly larger in inland regions. This result indicates that infrastructure investment can generate larger marginal returns where pre-existing infrastructure constraints are more binding.
4.5.3. Corporate governance structure heterogeneity.

The benefits of improved infrastructure may depend not only on external conditions but also on enterprises’ ability to respond to them. A more concentrated decision-making structure can reduce internal coordination costs and facilitate the rapid allocation of financial, technological, and human resources when external operating conditions improve. CEO-chair duality may therefore enable enterprises to translate improved electricity conditions into AI-related investment more rapidly, whereas separated leadership may involve greater coordination in resource adjustment. Thus, we expect the effect of UHV transmission projects to be stronger for enterprises with CEO-chair duality.

To examine this possibility, we construct a binary indicator (Dual), which equals 1 when the chairman and general manager positions are held by the same person and 0 otherwise. Columns (5)-(6) of Table 7 show that UHV transmission projects significantly promote enterprises’ AI development in both groups, while the coefficient difference test indicates a significantly larger effect for enterprises with CEO-chair duality. This finding suggests that enterprises’ organizational responsiveness affects their ability to convert infrastructure improvements into AI-related investment.
4.5.4. Industry heterogeneity.

The effect of energy infrastructure may further depend on enterprises’ technological intensity and absorptive capacity. High-tech enterprises generally have stronger digital foundations, greater demand for computing-intensive R&D, and greater capacity to integrate new technologies into production and innovation activities. Therefore, improved electricity availability and reliability can be more readily converted into AI investment and application in these enterprises. By contrast, enterprises with lower dependence on computing-intensive technologies may derive smaller marginal gains from the same infrastructure improvement. Thus, we expect the effect of UHV transmission projects on AI development to be stronger for high-tech enterprises.

To test this expectation, we construct a binary indicator (High-tech), which equals 1 for high-tech enterprises and 0 otherwise. Following the Classification of High-tech Manufacturing Industries issued by the National Bureau of Statistics of China (2017) and the revised Industry Classification Guidelines for Listed Companies issued by the China Securities Regulatory Commission (2012), six relevant industries are classified as high-tech industries. Columns (7)-(8) of Table 7 show that UHV transmission projects significantly promote enterprises’ AI development in both groups, with the coefficient difference test indicating a significantly larger effect for high-tech enterprises. The result supports the view that energy infrastructure creates greater value when it is complemented by stronger technological absorption and application capabilities.

Overall, the heterogeneity results support the two theoretical considerations outlined above. The marginal benefits of energy infrastructure are greater where pre-existing resource or infrastructure constraints are more binding, as reflected in the stronger effects among non-SOEs and inland enterprises. At the same time, the conversion of infrastructure improvements into AI development depends on enterprises’ internal capabilities, with stronger effects observed among enterprises with more responsive governance structures and greater technological intensity. These findings suggest that the value of energy infrastructure is jointly shaped by constraint relief and capability complementarity.
5. Further analyses
5.1. Mechanism tests

Building on the theoretical analysis, we further examine the channels through which UHV transmission projects affect enterprises’ AI development from the technological, organizational, and environmental dimensions of the TOE framework. Specifically, we consider technological innovation capability, organizational resource base, and regional financial development. Following the approach of Baron and Kenny (1986) [65], we examine the proposed mechanisms by estimating the effects of UHV transmission projects on the corresponding mechanism variables and then incorporating these variables into the baseline specification. The mechanism models are specified as follows:

5.1.1. Technological dimension.

Reliable electricity supply provides an important infrastructure condition for sustained R&D and computing-intensive innovation. We therefore examine whether UHV transmission projects promote enterprises’ AI development by strengthening technological innovation. Following previous studies [66,67], we employ two measures of technological innovation: the number of AI-related invention patent applications (Patent_AI) and the number of jointly applied green utility model patents (Patent_Green), which capture innovation quality and the sustainability of innovation activities, respectively.

Columns (1) and (3) of Table 8 show that the coefficients of UHV are significantly positive at the 10% and 1% levels, respectively. This indicates that UHV transmission projects are associated with greater AI-related inventive activity and collaborative technological innovation. In Columns (2) and (4), the coefficients of Patent_AI and Patent_Green are both significantly positive at the 1% level, while the coefficient of UHV remains significantly positive.

Stable electricity supply not only supports current production but also creates more favorable conditions for continuous R&D, experimentation, and technology iteration. The results therefore provide support for the technological channel proposed in Hypothesis 2a.
5.1.2. Organizational dimension.

AI development requires substantial internal resources for computing infrastructure, data accumulation, specialized personnel, and long-term R&D. Improvements in electricity supply can reduce energy-related operating burdens and production disruptions, thereby preserving resources that enterprises can allocate to technology investment. Therefore, we examine whether UHV transmission projects promote AI development by expanding enterprises’ organizational resource base. Following Arbelo et al. [68], we use organizational resource capacity (Org_Size), measured as the natural logarithm of total assets, to capture the overall resources available within the enterprise to support long-term investment.

Column (5) of Table 8 shows that the coefficient of UHV is significantly positive at the 5% level, suggesting that UHV transmission projects contribute to the expansion of enterprises’ internal resource base. When Org_Size is included in the AI regression in Column (6), its coefficient is significantly positive at the 1% level, while the coefficient of UHV remains significantly positive.

These results indicate that the benefits of improved energy infrastructure extend beyond the direct use of electricity. By reducing production disruptions and energy-related operating burdens, UHV transmission projects can help enterprises preserve and accumulate internal resources. Such resource accumulation is important for AI development because computing infrastructure, specialized personnel, and long-cycle R&D require substantial upfront commitments before technological returns can be realized. Therefore, a stronger internal resource base enhances enterprises’ capacity to sustain AI investment and absorb the associated risks, providing support for Hypothesis 2b.
5.1.3. Environmental dimension.

AI development also depends on external conditions that shape enterprises’ access to long-term financing. A more developed regional financial system can reduce financing frictions and facilitate access to external capital, thereby providing greater support for capital-intensive and long-cycle technology investment. Therefore, we examine regional financial development as an external financing channel. Following Zhang et al. [69], we measure city-level financial development (City_Fin) as the ratio of year-end deposits of financial institutions to regional GDP. A higher value indicates a greater availability of financial resources relative to the size of the local economy.

Column (7) of Table 8 shows that the coefficient of UHV is significantly positive at the 1% level, indicating that UHV transmission projects are associated with higher regional financial development. In Column (8), the coefficient of City_Fin is significantly positive at the 1% level, while the coefficient of UHV remains significantly positive.

These findings suggest that the influence of energy infrastructure can extend beyond enterprises’ internal operations to the broader external resource environment. By supporting regional production and investment activities, improvements in electricity supply may create more favorable conditions for the allocation of financial resources. Greater regional financial development, in turn, facilitates enterprises’ access to external capital required for AI-related R&D, computing investment, and technology deployment. This is particularly relevant to AI because large and uncertain technology investments may be difficult to sustain solely through internally generated resources. Therefore, the results provide support for the environmental channel proposed in Hypothesis 2c.
5.2. Misallocation correction effect

Constraints in traditional electricity transmission can create spatial frictions in energy allocation and further affect enterprises’ allocation of innovation resources. We consider two dimensions of such distortions. First, unstable energy supply may interact with financing constraints and limit enterprises’ ability to sustain large-scale and long-term AI investment, resulting in scale-related resource allocation distortions. Second, under greater operating and financial pressure, enterprises may prioritize resources for short-term production rather than long-term innovation, creating a structural imbalance in resource allocation [70]. By improving cross-regional electricity allocation and supply stability, UHV transmission projects may help alleviate these distortions.

For the scale dimension, we use the absolute value of the SA index from the CSMAR database to measure financing constraints, with a higher value indicating tighter constraints. Enterprises are divided into high- and low-financing-constraint groups using the industry-year median. Columns (1)-(2) of Table 9 show that the coefficient of UHV is significantly positive in both groups, while the effect is significantly larger for enterprises with lower financing constraints. This suggests that improvements in energy infrastructure do not automatically translate into greater AI investment when financing constraints remain binding. Enterprises facing lower financing constraints are better able to convert improved electricity conditions into sustained AI investment and application. This points to a complementarity between infrastructure improvement and financial capacity: UHV transmission projects can alleviate energy-side constraints, but adequate financial resources remain important for realizing the innovation benefits of improved infrastructure.

5.3. Shortboard complementing effect

The preceding analysis shows that UHV transmission projects can improve the allocation of energy and innovation resources. We further examine whether their benefits are greater where local development conditions provide weaker support for enterprises’ AI activities. Limitations in traditional electricity transmission may be particularly consequential in cities with weaker economic growth momentum or in less concentrated markets, where local economic and market conditions may provide relatively limited support for technology-intensive activities. By expanding the spatial reach of electricity supply and improving its stability, UHV transmission projects may partly compensate for these constraints and provide more favorable conditions for electricity- and computing-intensive AI activities. Therefore, we expect the marginal effect of UHV transmission projects to be greater where local development constraints are more binding.

To test this proposition, we consider two dimensions of local development conditions: urban economic growth (GDP) and market concentration (HHI). GDP is measured by the city-level GDP growth rate divided by 100, with a lower value indicating weaker local economic growth momentum. HHI is calculated as the sum of the squared shares of each enterprise’s owners’ equity in total industry owners’ equity, with a lower value indicating a less concentrated market structure. By improving access to stable cross-regional electricity supply, UHV transmission projects can partly compensate for weaknesses in local development conditions and broaden the infrastructure base available for enterprises’ AI activities. In this sense, energy infrastructure not only improves resource allocation efficiency but may also help narrow differences in the external conditions supporting technological transformation.

6. Conclusions and implications
6.1. Conclusions

This study uses the staggered rollout of UHV transmission projects across Chinese prefecture-level cities as a quasi-natural experiment to examine how energy infrastructure affects enterprises’ AI development. The results show that UHV transmission projects significantly promote enterprises’ AI development, and this finding remains robust across alternative specifications, measurement approaches, and endogeneity tests. Further analysis based on the TOE framework indicates that energy infrastructure facilitates AI development through three complementary channels: strengthening enterprises’ technological innovation, expanding their organizational resource base, and improving regional financial development. The effects also vary across enterprises with different ownership, location, governance structures, and technological characteristics.

These findings reveal that the role of energy infrastructure extends beyond the conventional function of electricity supply. By improving the reliability and allocation of electricity resources, UHV transmission projects create favorable conditions for sustained technological investment and the adoption of computing-intensive technologies. More broadly, the evidence suggests that enterprises’ AI development depends not only on algorithms, data, and computing capabilities, but also on the physical infrastructure that supports their continuous operation. Therefore, energy infrastructure constitutes an important foundation for the diffusion and development of AI at the enterprise level.
6.2. Managerial and policy implications

Our findings have implications for both enterprise management and public policy. At the enterprise level, reliable electricity supply should be regarded not merely as a production input but as an important condition for sustained AI investment. Therefore, managers should incorporate energy security into long-term digital strategies and coordinate AI investment with R&D, computing capacity, and internal resource allocation. Such coordination can help enterprises better translate improvements in electricity infrastructure into technological innovation and organizational capacity, thereby strengthening the foundations for sustained AI development.

At the policy level, energy infrastructure planning should be more closely aligned with regional digital and innovation strategies. The heterogeneous effects identified in this study suggest that infrastructure investment should not follow a uniform approach. Cross-regional electricity allocation should be improved to alleviate structural mismatches, while greater attention should be directed toward regions facing weaker economic conditions or other development bottlenecks. For developing economies, the findings further indicate that AI policy should extend beyond algorithms, data, and computing facilities to include the energy systems that support their continuous operation. Where fiscal and resource constraints are binding, phased and regionally targeted infrastructure investment may provide a more feasible path toward building the physical foundations for enterprises’ AI development.
6.3. Limitations and research prospects

Despite these findings, several limitations remain. First, the sample is restricted to Chinese listed enterprises, which generally have greater financing capacity, organizational resources, and technological capabilities than smaller or non-listed firms. Therefore, the findings may not fully capture how energy infrastructure affects AI development among enterprises facing more severe resource constraints. Future research could incorporate non-listed enterprises or survey-based microdata to examine whether the effects vary across a broader range of enterprises. Second, although we conduct several measurement-based robustness tests, the annual-report indicator remains a disclosure-based proxy for AI development. Future studies could combine textual measures with AI-related patents, investment, recruitment, or actual technology deployment data to provide a more multidimensional assessment. Finally, the longer-term and broader spillover effects of UHV transmission projects remain insufficiently explored. Energy infrastructure may influence AI development beyond directly connected enterprises through supply chains, industrial linkages, and cross-regional knowledge or resource flows. Extending the observation period and incorporating spatial or network-based approaches would help clarify the persistence and wider diffusion of these effects.

blocks.text: Abstract

Fever in the returning traveller is a challenging presentation that requires a wide array of clinical expertise and draws on complex medical decision-making. Recent advancements in artificial intelligence have shown it can be a helpful clinical support tool in this context. This scoping review, conducted in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses extension for Scoping Reviews guidelines and registered on the Open Science Framework (https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/BSPKX), aimed to identify the current state of artificial intelligence use in assessing fever in the returning traveller. Here we describe the three eligible studies evaluating three distinct AI approaches identified in the literature. These heterogenous studies reported promising performance on study-specific endpoints in controlled settings. Given the lack of external validation, narrow populations studied, and absence of real-world implementation or user acceptance testing, further research is needed to explore this technology in a real-world clinical setting. The limited available evidence suggests that AI may have future potential to support assessment of fever in the returning traveller; however, clinical utility, safety, and real-world effectiveness remain unestablished. Large language models represent an emerging area of interest but were not evaluated in the studies included in this review.
Introduction

Fever in the returning traveller (FRT) is a common but often challenging presentation given its broad differential diagnosis [1]. It is estimated that 25% of Canadians returning from travel may experience a travel-related illness [2,3]. Prompt and accurate assessment of these presentations is essential as they can be associated with diseases such as malaria, dengue, typhoid, and TB [4]. Globalization, increased rates of post pandemic travel, as well as recent emerging diseases such as the COVID-19, Zika, and Chikungunya have highlighted the growing complexity of diagnosing infectious diseases in returning travelers [4,5].

Currently, febrile illness in the returning traveller is assessed through a detailed history, physical examination, and pathogen-specific investigations [2]. This approach relies on front-line clinicians having a high level of clinical expertise in travel and tropical medicine, emerging diseases, and general infectious diseases.

Artificial intelligence (AI), though in its infancy as a clinical tool, is already integrated into electronic medical record platforms to assist with documentation, summarizing complex conversations and developing clinical plans [6]. It has demonstrated potential in clinical diagnostics and risk prediction, with effective emergent tools spanning from breast cancer diagnosis through mammograms analysis algorithms to detection of pneumonia on chest radiography [7]. AI models are uniquely positioned to synthesize large amounts of data for clinicians including data such as regional outbreak data, pathogen specific geography, or incubation periods of pathogens [8]. This information is essential for accurate clinical diagnosis but can be difficult and time-consuming to access during brief routine patient care. Such technology could be leveraged to guide clinical decision-making by generating a comprehensive differential diagnosis, for example, allowing clinicians to use their clinical judgment to determine the final diagnosis.

Developing AI tools to assess FRT can support clinical decision-making to overcome the need to integrate vast amounts of clinical and non-clinical information into assessments. Ultimately this may provide the avenue to develop new tools to aid in the timely diagnosis and management of FRT. Despite its potential, there are currently few studied clinical applications of AI within infectious diseases, and the extent of its use specifically in FRT remains unclear.

This scoping review aims to examine the current use of AI in assessing FRT. By synthesizing the available evidence, this review offers important insights into the current uses of AI in this context, its potential benefits, limitations, and key considerations.
Methods
Ethics Statement
This scoping review synthesized data from previously published studies. Research ethics board review and informed consent were therefore not required.

This scoping review was structured in adherence to the PRISMA-ScR (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses extension for Scoping Reviews) guidelines (See S1 Table). This study was registered within the Open Science Framework (OSF) database (https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/BSPKX). A scoping review methodology was chosen to map the available evidence in an emerging and heterogenous field, given initial literature searches demonstrated a lack of recent reviews addressing our research question [9].
Literature search

An initial search of MEDLINE (Ovid) was undertaken to identify articles. This was used to identify keywords and terms to develop the full search strategy. The search strategy was peer-reviewed by a university research librarian. Our search strategy encompassed four concepts: artificial intelligence, infectious diseases, fever, and returning travellers. The search design involved identification of synonyms for these concepts as well as Boolean operators. No search filters were used to limit the search results. The search strategy used is available through OSF as part of the published study protocol.

The databases searched include MEDLINE (Ovid), EMBASE (Ovid), Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), and Web of Science databases. Sources of unpublished studies and gray literature were not included. Searches included records published in the databases from their inception up the time of data collection which was February 07, 2025.
Eligibility criteria

This scoping review considered both experimental and quasi-experimental study designs including randomized controlled trials and non-randomized controlled trials. Observational studies including prospective and retrospective cohort studies, case-control studies and cross-sectional studies were included.

Inclusion criteria: Studies including adult patients who are returning travellers from any length of foreign travel from their home country with an infectious disease(s) as a cause of fever. Studies must use of a form of AI explicitly in the context of infectious disease assessment, including history, physical, diagnosis, clinical decision support, risk stratification, and/or management to be included. For this scoping review, AI was defined broadly to include both rule-based expert systems and machine learning approaches, which were grouped for mapping purposes but interpreted as distinct methods. Studies must have outcomes related to diagnostic accuracy, predictive value, efficiency, clinical utility, or impact of AI in clinical practice. These outcomes did not have to pertain directly to the use of AI in clinical assessment. Studies must have occurred in healthcare, research, or academic settings to be included.

Exclusion criteria: Studies focusing on non-travel-related fever or non-infectious causes of fever and studies with populations not defined as returning travellers were excluded. Studies including only paediatric patients were also excluded. Studies that did not specifically apply AI to the assessment of FRT or were situated in non-healthcare-related settings (ex. Training programs) were excluded.
Study selection

Covidence was used to manage the data outputted from the structured search strategy. Duplicates were removed and titles and abstracts were screened by two independent reviewers based on the inclusion/exclusion criteria. A full text review was conducted next with two independent reviewers. Reasons for exclusion were recorded. Disagreements between reviewers were resolved through discussion and a third reviewer where agreement could not be reached. The methodology is outlined in Fig 1 as a PRISMA diagram.

blocks.text: Data extraction

Data was extracted from the selected citations by independent reviewers using the Covidence platform. The data extracted included: authors; year of publication, article title, country in which the study conducted, study methods, study objective, study design, start and/or end date, if provided, study funding sources, possible conflicts of interest for study authors, population description, clinical setting, inclusion criteria, exclusion criteria, total number of participants, AI method(s), method architecture (if any), function of model (intended use), input data; output data (how does the output data support assessment of FRT), user acceptance; qualitative information on user acceptance of deployed models where reported, key qualitative and quantitative results reported, key contributions, author-reported limitation, and author-reported future directions. The full extracted data is provided in the supplementary appendix (S1 Table). Extracted data was synthesized using a narrative approach. A quality or risk of bias assessment was not conducted, given the scoping review was conducted using PRISMA-ScR methodology.
Results

1335 unique articles were identified from the literature search. Following title and abstract screening, 1324 articles were excluded, and 11 articles underwent full-text review by two reviewers independently. 8 articles were excluded. 1 included the wrong intervention, 3 included primarily pediatric populations, and 4 had no specific consideration of returning travellers. Three articles met inclusion criteria. Two were prospective cohort studies and one was an exploratory observational study. The studies were based in Belgium (n = 1), Sweden (n = 1), and one was an international multi-centre study including Spain, Belgium, Switzerland (n = 1).

The mean number of study participants was 354 (standard deviation [SD]: 355). Studies selected for patients over the age of 18 (n = 2) and unspecified (n = 1). All three studies selected for patients with febrile illness described as fever (≥37.5°C) or symptoms of fever (n = 1), fever >38°C (measured or self-reported) (n = 1), and unspecified (n = 1). Similarly, all three articles included patients that recently returned from international travel within the past year (n = 1), the past two months (n = 1) and unspecified (n = 1). No explicit exclusion criteria were listed for any of the studies. All studies were conducted in hospital settings (n = 3) and all were multi-year studies including multiple seasons (n = 3).
Model characteristics

Three unique architectures were used: GIDEON rule-based system (n = 1), boosting algorithms (i.e. XGBoost) (n = 1), a Boruta feature selection model, and random forest model with 5-fold and 10-fold cross-validation. (n = 1). The rule-based system provided an output of a ranked list of differential diagnoses, each with an associated probability [10]. The boosting algorithm, XGBoost (reduced to a six-feature model), outputted a binary classification of suspected malaria listed as ‘yes’ or ‘no’ [11]. The random forest model generated disease classification per patient [12].

The GIDEON rule-based expert system intended to provide a list of differential diagnoses to support the management of febrile illness in patients returning from recent travel. While area under the curve (AUC) was not listed for the GIDEON rule-based expert system, a diagnostic accuracy (correct diagnosis in top 5 outputs) of 64% in febrile cases with confirmed or probable infectious etiology was achieved. This was higher in cases of malaria, rickettsial, and dengue, reaching over 80%. Accuracy declines were noted with cases of amebic liver abscess and Plasmodium falciparum malaria, and in cases of greater than three clinical finding inputs [10].

The MALrisk algorithm (XGBoost reduced to a six-feature model) aimed to identify febrile patients at high risk of malaria in non-endemic settings. The MALrisk model achieved an AUC of 0.95 with a sensitivity of 100% (95% CI: 96–100) and specificity of 72% (95% CI: 68–75) in the test set and an AUC of 0.98 (F1 score of 0.78) in the training set [11].

The random forest model intended to differentiate specific infections in febrile returning travellers using immune signatures. This model achieved an AUC of 0.97 with some variation across models targeted towards specific pathologies such as bacterial gastroenteritis. AUC was seen to improve with addition of lab markers to the model. Generally, sensitivities and specificities were greater than 0.87 and 0.72, respectively [12].

None reported on user acceptance including data examining end-user engagement or real-world pilot testing. Data was not provided on clinician satisfaction, usability, or real-world complications/applicability.
Model variables

The specific data inputted in each model is listed in Supplementary S2 Table. Common variables inputted include epidemiological findings including location of travel and demographic data, specific symptoms, and laboratory values like platelet count and bilirubin. Other variables included were antimalarial chemoprophylaxis intake and plasma cytokine/chemokine levels, generally used due to the use-case of the associated model.
Discussion

AI methods may facilitate the simultaneous analysis of multiple clinical and epidemiological variables and therefore have potential utility in diagnostic decision support. This review identified three current published applications of AI applied to the assessment of FRT. Given the complexity of this presentation, and the many associated variables, AI may have a future role in supporting assessment; however, the current evidence remains preliminary. This systematic literature search identified three heterogenous applications of AI currently studied for use in the assessment of FRT. The included studies employed a rule-based model, a gradient boosting algorithm, and random forest model. Varying endpoints led models to produce unique outputs such as a list of differential diagnosis, identifying risk for suspected malaria, or differentiation of specific infections, respectively. These models reported promising performance in achieving their study-specific endpoints. The included studies demonstrate that distinct AI approaches can generate clinically interpretable outputs from structured inputs; however, reproducibility across populations, institutions, and clinical environments has not been established [10]. All three models highlight the potential utility and viability of AI support in clinical evaluation of patients returning from travel with consistency given standard inputs, but do not establish real-world effectiveness, safety, or scalability.
Model architecture

Each model utilized core principles of AI in clinical decision support, generally centered around decision trees, to produce their respective outputs. However, these architectures are not methodologically equivalent, particularly because the rule-based expert system relies on predefined logic while the machine learning models learn statistical patterns from data. The rule-based model employs a decision tree-like approach by following a set of defined rules to produce an outcome. For example, an input provided will traverse through a decision tree similar to decision trees used by clinicians. The gradient boosting algorithm is fundamentally a compilation of many decisions-trees to identify errors in previous predictions and produce the best possible output. These are developed through sequential training to identify such errors as opposed to defining rules. Finally, a random forest model uses multiple decision trees to produce a large group of outputs that are then compiled by the model to produce a final output.

The intricacies of the input data used as a basis for the models varied significantly. For example, the random forest model designed to differentiate between specific infections used plasma cytokine/chemokine levels as one of its variables, a value not often used in standard clinical practice [12]. Due to the limited literature on such levels and the lack of existing models leveraging these values, this model generated novel interpretations for applications in a clinical setting. Indirectly, this model provided insight into the correlation between specific pathologies and proteomics - information that may become more available and useful in clinical practice within the context of such models. For example, an elevated IL10, sCD25, and sTNFRI, and reduced sCD40L were found to be associated with malaria [12]. While not part of routine clinical testing for malaria, these markers have been well studied in the basic science realm, and within the context of a comprehensive clinical model may lead to more accurate prediction scores than currently available.

None of the models used greater than six categories of variables as input data. This may be a reflection of the context limitations of existing AI architectures that begin to see a plateau or even decline in performance when given too many parameters to correlate [11]. The MALrisk model identifies reduction to six variables from an initial boosting algorithm as potentially supportive of future implementation by reducing the number of required inputs. Fewer variables may reduce data entry and computational requirements; however, the included study did not evaluate whether this translated into greater clinician uptake, scalability, or implementation success [11]. As the capabilities advance, it is possible that more variables will be included. These advancements may enable newer algorithms to improve the accuracy of their outputs, though this requires empirical validation in FRT.

Similar to input data, the nature of output data varied between models. The GIDEON rule-based system, developed a list of differential diagnoses and included ‘why-not’ and ‘compare’ functions that provided further explanations for the outputs produced [10]. Alternatively, the MALrisk model produced a binary output (yes/no) to identify a suspected malaria case [11]. From the perspective of model functions, inputs and outputs both require interpretation, analysis and synthesis of the data provided, however, they do hold differing practical implications. A detailed list of differential diagnoses with included explanations can provide higher-level clinical decision-making support for healthcare providers aiming to expand their diagnoses and management plans. Alternatively, a binary output can support short-term actions such as empiric treatments, reporting, testing, and transfer to appropriate facilities. Both output models may have applicability for ruling in/out high-risk conditions (e.g., malaria) and capturing broader differential diagnoses to not miss less common presentations or pathogens. Both applications highlight the importance of catering model outputs tailored to a clinically useful endpoint.
Model limitations

Despite the results of the models, there remain limitations of their applicability.  Firstly, models were not used in clinical pilot studies and there was no end-user engagement resulting in the lack of data surrounding clinical applicability, clinician satisfaction, and real-world errors.  This limits the ability to identify the feasibility of model integration in frontline healthcare settings that may experience unique constraints like time, delayed charting, and limited history from patients.  The mean number of study participants was 354 (standard deviation [SD]: 355) with most articles identifying a lack of diversity within the study population, limiting the generalizability of the application of these models.  External validation was also limited, further restricting conclusions about performance outside the original study settings.  As with many AI models in healthcare, the opportunity to use them in pilot studies remains limited [6].  This stems from multiple systems-based limitations like the lack of healthcare policies on AI use as well as little infrastructure to support its integration (ex.  technical support team with training in AI clinical decision support systems).

Clinicians continue to have concerns regarding the implications of AI on clinical judgement and workflow, often concerned about errors that may be produced [13].  For example, MALrisk had a misclassification rate of 28% for non-malarial febrile patients [11].  The GIDEON rule-based system missed 31 total diagnoses, 11 of which were severe or life-threatening such as Plasmodium falciparum malaria [10].  Beyond this, limitations exist intrinsically within the architecture of these models.  The variables chosen and the specific data inputted can be biased based on the data collector, inputter, or designer of these models.  For example, the specificity of the travel region inputted can provide different levels of context to an AI model.  Stating ‘sub-Saharan Africa’ may develop different correlations compared to stating a specific country.  Study design in AI model development also comes with risk of bias.  For example, while the selection of a boosting algorithm to develop MALrisk is largely appropriate, similar results may be achieved with other forms of AI, especially considering recent evolution.
Advancements in artificial intelligence

Importantly, none of the three studies included in this review evaluated large language models (LLMs); therefore, the following discussion reflects emerging opportunities for future research rather than evidence identified through this review. With the recent advent of highly capable, publicly accessible large language models (LLMs), the production of models to support clinical decision-making has become increasingly simple. Recent literature has shown that LLMs can perform at the same level or better than physicians when providing written responses to healthcare questions spanning multiple domains [14]. There exists significant potential for clinical applications of models to support clinical decision-making in the context of FRT by leveraging this technology, but this remains speculative in FRT. To address concerns around patient safety and medical errors, the use of virtual patients produced using LLMs provides a controlled, reproducible, high-fidelity environment for pilot testing [15]. Beyond this, true pilot testing in real-world scenarios is essential to the further development of this technology.
Clinical applications

Development of AI models to assess FRT may offer opportunities to support clinicians who must integrate substantial clinical and epidemiological information. Clinicians face significant levels of burnout driven by increasing levels of charting, electronic data review, and administrative work [16]. AI models that support clinical synthesis for decision-making are a well-positioned tool clinicians may be able to leverage in making real-time decisions in the future if validated and safely integrated into clinical workflows. These studies suggest that relatively simple models can generate potentially useful clinical outputs in controlled settings; however, none of the included studies established improvements in patient outcomes or clinical decision-making. Such models could potentially be adapted for use across different healthcare settings, but cost-effectiveness, scalability, and implementation were not evaluated in the included studies [14,15]. In a primary care setting, such models may be able to aid clinicians in identifying the most likely cause of FRT and guide potential next steps. These models may help inform when referral is warranted as well as information to provide [17,18]. Overall, this represents a potential future application, but effects on clinician workload, treatment timeliness, resource utilization, and patient outcomes require prospective evaluation.
Future directions

Given the application of AI clinical support models remain in their early stages, further research is needed to explore their applicability and assess their limitations in the context of assessing FRT. Despite our broad literature search, only three applications were identified in this setting. This may be partly due to the relative infancy of AI in medicine as well as hesitancy for adoption, including healthcare policy limitations, lack of existing infrastructure and clinician concerns surrounding reliability [13]. Studies using a wider variety of AI methods, such as LLMs, applied in controlled simulation environments followed by externally validated prospective studies could help establish whether these approaches have clinical value in FRT. Further advances in LLM capabilities may warrant future investigation for clinical decision support, although their role in FRT remains untested [14]. For example, LLMs with these capabilities may be able to produce a list of differential diagnoses and key next steps for a management plan based on a history, physical examination and brief investigations inputted by a clinician.
Limitations

Several limitations exist in this scoping review, primarily, the lack of literature in this context limits the ability to draw broader conclusions on the use of AI to assess FRT. Additionally, as a scoping review, this study was designed to map available evidence rather than formally compare effectiveness. Secondly, due to the heterogeneity of the studies included, such as differing models, statistical measures, and variable endpoints, a true comparison between performance could not be accurately assessed. The rapid evolution of AI technologies may also affect the relevance of individual models over time and complicate comparisons across studies conducted in different technological eras. This scoping review simply maps the current landscape and synthesizes the early developments in this field. While limited by the available evidence, this review establishes a foundation for future research on the role of AI in assessing FRT, rather than evidence of clinical readiness.
Conclusion

FRT remains a diagnostically challenging presentation demanding focused clinical expertise and skill for accurate diagnosis and efficient management. AI-based decision-support approaches may eventually assist clinicians managing this complex presentation, but their effects on diagnostic accuracy, clinician workload, and patient outcomes have not yet been established in real-world FRT care. This scoping review identified three studies evaluating distinct AI approaches for the assessment of FRT, each reporting promising performance on study-specific outcomes in controlled settings. These findings should be considered preliminary and demonstrate proof-of-concept rather than clinical readiness, effectiveness, or scalability. Further research incorporating, external validation, prospective clinical evaluation, user acceptance testing, implementation assessment, and safety evaluation, will be essential to understand whether and how these tools can be safely integrated into clinical care.
Key points

Artificial intelligence has been used for assessment of fever in the returning traveller with models reporting promising performance won study-specific outcomes in controlled settings, though evidence remains limited and heterogenous.
